utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can I ask for the appearances, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ken Scott, Vassily Poryvaev, and our case manager Skye Winner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me turn to the Defence counsel whom we are familiar with, but, for the record, can you please introduce yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. President, Your Honours. Michael Karnavas for Mr. Jadranko Prlic, along with Suzana Tomanovic, co-counsel, and Ana Vlahovic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Senka Nozica, Defence counsel for Mr. Bruno Stojic; and in the courtroom we have the legal assistant or court manager Valent Slonje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Bozidar Kovacic for Slobodan Praljak together with co-counsel Mrs. Nika Pinter and case manager Valentina Ivic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Vesna Alaburic for Milivoj Petkovic, appearing with case manager Davor Lazic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I'm Tomislav Jonjic, Defence counsel for Valentin Coric, appointed. Next to me, legal advisor Krystyna Grinberg and case manager Ida Jurkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Mr. Pusic, Roger Sahota, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today is Wednesday, the 3rd of May. I greet everybody; the accused, the counsel, the Prosecution, and all the people supporting our work. In particular, I greet Madam Witness who is going to continue her testimony, and she is first going to answer the Prosecution's questions. But before I give the floor to you, Mr. Mundis, I have two pieces of information to convey to you. Mr. Mundis, first of all, we received from the Prosecution an additional list of documents under Rule 65 ter. They are numbered from 9.411 to 9.424. I'd like to have the binder. The binder. I want to have a hard copy of those documents. Second thing: After the examination-in-chief, the time will come for cross-examination. As you know, Mr. Praljak had asked for leave to possibly put questions himself. We issued a ruling a few days ago, and we answered his request. We said that when an accused has a specific scope of knowledge or know-how, on the basis of his experience, could possibly put questions. We also said in our decision that further to Rule 85, an accused could also testify as a witness. It is provided for by the Rules. Furthermore, practically, unfortunately, this courtroom is not the best venue for this, but when it is question time, if an accused wants to raise the attention of his counsel on a specific thing, he can do so by scribbling a note, passing it on through a security officer to the counsel in question, because as you know, unfortunately, your clients are far away from you. I don't know who was initially the designer for this courtroom, but they didn't think that an accused might feel the need to speak to his lawyer. What should have been done is sort of having an accused next to his lawyer, as you can see in the States or somewhere else, but not like tens of metres away. I also find it difficult with regard to the legal assistants, the legal officers. I can't see them, and I can't communicate with them. But, well, the architects of courtrooms, they could have asked for expertise, expertise in terms of criminal design, as it were, or criminal court design. So it's difficult for an accused to communicate with his lawyer through little notes. We shall try to adjust to the situation in order to best meet the needs and on the basis of these new conditions. This being said, Mr. Mundis, you now have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, yesterday we ended the day's sitting in private session, and that was done, as Your Honours are well aware, because of the potential for identifying specific victims. I'm going to return to that issue of the identities of the women who were detained with this witness, but perhaps, given the large number of names that she's identified, perhaps we could do that in open session and then only go into private session when we're specifically talking about -- about victims, because there's a large number of names that she has identified and we don't believe that that necessarily needs to be in private session, although when we go to specifics about any of those particular victims and what may or may not have happened to them, we would then ask to move into private session. And so with the leave of the Chamber, I would propose that we go forward in open session. I will be asking the witness some follow-up questions with respect to the witnesses that she identified yesterday in closed session, but before I do that, I want to make sure that I'm not revealing anything that shouldn't have been revealed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. No problem at all. In the event that a name is mentioned, the name of a potential victim, I would -- I could always give an order to make changes. Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So good morning, Ms. Drljevic.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ma'am, you just heard what I just discussed with the Presiding Judge, and I want to make sure you absolutely understand what we're going to do. I'm going to ask you some follow-up questions concerning the women that you talked about yesterday. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I don't want you to tell us anything about what happened to any of these people until we're able to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So that these preliminary questions I'm going to ask you will only go towards the identity and perhaps the ages of the people that we'll be talking about. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fine. Yes, I do understand. I'm not quite sure that I won't be repeating a name or perhaps leave a name out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, let's start, then, by recapping what you told us yesterday. You told us that you arrived on the 8th of June, 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may lodge an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. What's your problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's not a problem, it's an observation. Mr. Mundis is now about to summarise what we heard yesterday. We certainly don't need the Prosecutor summarising the testimony of a witness. We have the transcript. I think if we could just pose the questions and get to it, it might be a little bit easier. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understood that the Prosecutor was about to ask again for the list of the names of people who were with the witness. Was that your intention? You were not going to give names for her to confirm them, were you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the witness yesterday identified a number of people, and some of those people she indicated approximate ages. We're proposing to ask her if she can identify and give us the approximate ages of the remaining people that she identified yesterday for whom she didn't give us an approximate age. So I am planning on asking her about each and every one of those women that she identified yesterday for whom she did not specify an approximate age, and I'll then go on and ask her if there's anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, yesterday you mentioned Hasiba Grebovic. Do you recall approximately how old she was in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time she was about 40 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, yesterday afternoon you mentioned the name of Helena Brkic. Do you recall approximately how old Ms. Brkic was in June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 18 and 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, yesterday you mentioned a person by the name of Mrs. Savic. Do you recall approximately how old she was in June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, over 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yesterday, Ms. Drljevic, you mentioned a person by the name of Sefika Basic. Do you recall approximately the age of Ms. Basic in June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 50 and 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yesterday, Ms. Drljevic, you mentioned someone by the name of Nada Mitric. Do you recall approximately what age Ms. Mitric was in June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Razija Gosto. Do you recall her approximate age in June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also about 50 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about Mubera Micijevic? Do you recall her approximate age in June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Micijevic. 45, 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lejla Micijevic, do you recall her approximate age in June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 20. About 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Elvedina or Eca Hodzic. Approximately what age was she in June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Her surname is Klinac. Her mother's name is Hodzic. She was 40, 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Rabija Hadzic. Do you recall her approximate age in June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mejra Demirovic. Do you recall her approximate age in June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also between 45 and 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Fata Kubic. Do you recall the approximate age of Fata Kubic in June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also 45, 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, other than the names of the people we've mentioned this morning and yesterday afternoon, do you recall the names or approximate -- and approximate ages of any of the other people who were detained during the period you were in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In -- or, rather, after the 15th of July, 1993, they brought in a woman named Nena. She was about 70 years old. Her surname was Feriz. And with her, two children, a boy of 4 and a girl of 6. I think their names were Anel and Amela. Then there was Mrs. Mersija Mersa Krzic. She was brought in from Samica. Otherwise, she's from Maglaj. She was about 45 years old; 40 to 45. Yesterday, I think I mentioned Dr. Kreso's mother. She was about 50. And I think I mentioned Mrs. Hodzic, Esadina's mother, and she was 80 -- well, 75 to 80. Then there was three sisters by the name of Pilav; Jasmina, about 40 years old. I don't know what Zela's real name was. Her nickname was Zela. She was 25 to 30 years old. Then there was Ema. She was between 20 and 25. And a relation of theirs, Elvedina. She was, I think, 17 or 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, you've mentioned a boy of 4 and a girl of 6, and you indicated you think their names were Anel and Amela. Were these two children the youngest people detained in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. As far as I know. But in August or September another woman was brought in, and her name was Advija, and she brought a small girl with her. The girl was 9. And her other daughter, she was about 18, 18 to 20. As well as a son. His name was Narcis, and he was accommodated in the male section, and I think he was 17 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: These younger people that you've told us about, where in Heliodrom were they kept?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the children I mentioned or, rather, the younger people, were in the rooms with us, together with the women, except for Narcis. He was in the male dormitories. But this woman, Nena Feriz, with her grandchildren, she said that she had spent two or three days in the cellar in solitary confinement cells.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or "Samica" might be a place, interpreter's note. Could the witness clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you clarify your last answer, please, in terms of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Samica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- "Samica."

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were premises in the cellar of the building. Solitary confinement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they had bars on the windows. I don't know whether you can see them on the photograph that you showed yesterday. Very small windows, about 30 to 40 centimetres high. And that was the only way the light could get into that room. There was a concrete floor with a metal pail for the people to relieve themselves in, and a very thin rubber mattress.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, these women and the children that you've told us about this morning, how long were they detained in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nena Feriz and her two children, as I've already said, came after the 15th of July. I know the date, because it's linked to an operation in Kocina, the military operation in Kocina. So they were captured on that particular occasion. When they arrived -- or, rather, when the Red Cross arrived in August, 1993, they were taken away to a house of some kind, and then they were returned. And sometime in October, they were taken away - I learnt this later - to a house in the Rudnik area, which is the northern part of Mostar, and I don't know when they were transferred to Ploce subsequently. Advija and her daughters, Azra [phoen] and Nina, arrived in September and stayed roughly until -- well, August or September. And they stayed for about two months, and according to what they later said when I left the camp later on, they were put up in a house of some sort at Rudnik, and then they were transferred to the left bank before I was released myself. That is to say, before December, 1993. Narcis stayed on until the 17th -- well, I don't know when Narcis was released. He stayed on, anyway, after them. I don't know whether he was released in that group of civilians in December or whether he remained until March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, I'd like to ask you now about the conditions that existed in Heliodrom at the time you were detained there. Can you please tell us about the living conditions in the building where you were detained from June until December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, we were put up in two rooms in the attic area, and there were about 10 to 12 beds in each room. We had a bed with a foam mattress, and when it became cold later on - that was perhaps in October or November; I know that it was snowing on one occasion - we were given something to cover ourselves with, a blanket. We did not have a bathroom. I know that the men downstairs on the first floor, on the ground floor, was where there was a bathroom. On two occasions they took us there to have a bath on the ground floor -- in the ground floor bathroom, and twice to the cellar where there was a kitchen with a large -- large concrete baths where we were able to bathe. At the entrance, that is to say opposite our rooms, there were two smaller rooms. In one of them we saw some tables, to begin with, and a gynaecological examination table. And later on, they allowed two of the women inmates to turn that into a little room for themselves. And in the other room next to the staircase was an improvised makeshift kitchen with a wash basin. So that Novica, who was a Serb, he was one of the detainees but a free man, said that those premises had been built on, or, rather, refurbished in 1992. Otherwise, before that it was just an attic space without these rooms. At the end of the corridor -- or, rather, next to these two little rooms there was one more room where old military uniforms were stored. And next to that there was a toilet. Well, it was just a squatting toilet, in actual fact, just a hole and two places to put your feet on. Some women tried to wash themselves there by throwing water over themselves, but then later on the people who brought in food to us, we were informed that there was -- that when we tried to wash ourselves like that the water would just flow down and go down the walls of the rooms in which the men were sleeping. Anyway, in this makeshift kitchen there was a small electric hotplate and a pan, a big pan, in which we were able to wash and boil our clothes in. There were a lot of us there, and we had just one or two changes of clothing. We would wash -- well, when there was some water there, we'd wash there. When there wasn't any water, they would allow us to bring water up from the ground floor because there was always water on the ground floor. So we did this. We brought it up in bottles, so that we were able to wash ourselves to the waist over that wash basin, and from the waist down, well, we would place one foot in one pail and our other foot in the other pail and do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, if you need to take a short break, I'm sure the Trial Chamber would understand that and we can certainly accommodate you.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm fine, thanks. Please don't hold this against me. I will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I assure you, ma'am, that no one will hold this against you. Let me ask you about the -- because you mentioned food. Can you tell us a little bit about food and access to drinking water in Heliodrom when you were there.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were provided with two meals a day. In the morning we'd usually receive some sort of snack, something to spread on bread, sometimes some milk. But the food I was given was really very poor. It's the metal container that I disliked the most, the container that they put the food in. According to what the people who would bring the food in said, they said that the food that the women were provided with was significantly better than the food that the men were provided with. When I arrived in the camp, the detention conditions were very poor. I was provided with very bad food. I didn't eat well. And someone whom I knew from before and someone whom I spoke to asked me why I had become so weak. But the main problem for me was that container. It looked like a container one would use for dogs. He even offered to bring me some other utensils from his home, some other cutlery and crockery from home. So in any event, the doctor suggested I should be put on a drip in the military clinic on a number of occasions. The women who went to work would sometimes bring in a tin of food of some kind. That would often be tuna fish that had a bad smell. And as I said, I was in a poor state. And even when I was released later on, the food I ate was not much better. But it wasn't possible for me to eat in such conditions. Sometimes they'd give me biscuits or a tin of food, items that had been provided through humanitarian aid organisations. And this was really very exhausting for me, because we would lunch very early and there was no dinner. We would have lunch perhaps around noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, I'd like to change the focus slightly. I'd like to ask you now about how you and the other women that were detained in Heliodrom were treated. And again, if we need to go into private session, I'm sure the Trial Chamber will permit that. Can you please tell us how you were treated during the course of your detention in Heliodrom from June through December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially everyone found the situation a little strange since there were women there. Although I had already seen some women there and even before the conflict broke out on the 9th of May, 1993, a large group of women had been brought in, and they stayed there for two, three, or 10 days. They were then released through the intermediary of the international community. The people would often come, and they found this quite strange: I was the only member of the army. I was the only female member of the army. Everyone else there, they were all civilians. They would look at me as if I was some sort of a freak. But initially they didn't treat us badly. Up until the 30th of June, 1993, they spoke to us in a normal way, I could put it like that, although I felt there was some intolerance. I thought of Damir Sipar. I told him that I wanted to go out. I don't know whom he worked for, perhaps the military police. But in January, 1993, or in April, joint patrols was formed and fire was opened on a vehicle. And after this event he carried out an on-site investigation. And when I spoke to him on that occasion, well, it's difficult, you know. When you're in such a situation, you want to hold on to anything you can. Perhaps some would not be bothered by this, but I was really very much affected. His mother had been my teacher, and when I spoke to him I was perhaps trying to find some sort of protection. If someone had asked me whom I would have gone to visit on the right bank, I would have said his mother, but when we spoke to each other, well, he -- he said she'd taught a lot of students, and I then regretted having mentioned the fact that she had been my teacher. And on the 30th of June, my commander, Hujdur, was killed. I found out about that on that very same day. They brought in Dr. Kreso's mother on that day. And soldiers would often appear. They wouldn't even enter the room, they'd just look through the bars and ask us whether we regretted the fact that he had been killed. The most unpleasant situation I experienced was in September, after the 21st. I later found out about the date of the operation on Stotina. I didn't even know anything about what had happened at the time. Perhaps I found out something about the event on the following day. After the month of September, a group of soldiers arrived. Among them there was Robi Buhac, who was about 25 years old. He had long, curly hair at the time. He also asked me whether I was sorry that Hujka had been killed. Naturally, I said that, yes, I was sorry. Then he loaded his -- his rifle. It was loaded. Then -- in fact, that's what he did when I told him that he would feel sorry if his commander had been killed. And then another soldier, who also said that his name was Robi and that he was from Vukovar, appeared, and he told him to put the gun down. And then the same month, there were two individuals who were released towards the end of September. That's why I believe that all of this happened in September. One morning a young man called Veki appeared with a Heckler gun. I don't know his first and last name, but his mother is the guard Klemo -- Klemo's sister, and his father is a Serb. He treated me very roughly. He threw me into a chair in the corridor. He pointed the Heckler gun at me, and he asked me, "What do you want, Balija?" My -- I believe that two individuals persuaded him to act in this way. I wouldn't want to name them. That evening -- in the morning he was in camouflage uniform. In the evening, he appeared in a leather jacket. I remember that he had some kind of a sign on the back of the jacket, some sort of colourful sign. It looked like flames. He took me to a room on the floor below, because there were two or three small rooms there. I'd been interrogated in one of them. I know that there was a pharmacy in one of the rooms. We spoke to each other in an unformal way. We would first speak about ordinary things, and then he would suddenly ask me a specific question. He asked me how long I had been in the camp, whether I had had any contact with any of the guards, and this is something that never even crossed my mind. But when I said this was a matter of one's attitude or the thoughts one had, it was only at that point that he really went mad. He became very angry, and he said, "This is because you hate the Croats." I said that had nothing to do with national questions, and I said it was just a matter of the time or, rather, the conditions in which I was living. And this went on for about 10 or 15 minutes perhaps. He then took me out of the room. When he tried to open the door, he turn the light off, and he tried to approach me, to touch me. I pushed him away. He told me to put my arms down, to put my hands down, and that I should not forget the fact that I was just a prisoner. He tried to do this once more, perhaps twice. I pushed him away each time he made such an attempt, because this is not something I would do voluntarily. I would do everything I could to avoid being raped, since this is the worst thing that a woman can experience. He then said that he believed I hadn't been with anyone, and he took me back to the room. He said that I shouldn't mention what had happened to anyone. And naturally, I listened to his advice because five minutes later he appeared and took Jasmina Piljar away. A few days later she told me that he had treated her in the same way that he had treated me, and he immediately asked her how I had behaved upon returning to the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, if I could interrupt you at this point in time. Can you please tell us if you were aware of any other mistreatment of any of the other detainees that were kept in Heliodrom during the time period you were there?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the mistreatment of any of the other detainees, if you mean sexual mistreatment. I know that there was mistreatment elsewhere, but I know this through hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me move on to another subject, ma'am. You told us earlier this morning about a time period when the Red Cross came to Heliodrom. Do you recall approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in August, 1993. I don't know the exact date, but I do know that there was a woman whom I saw at the Heliodrom and who arrived in May. I do know that she wasn't registered until August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was this occasion in August, 1993, or approximately August, 1993, the only occasion in which Red Cross representatives came to Heliodrom during the time period that you were there?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They came on two or three other occasions but without any success. Because we would recognise their vehicles. We would recognise the vehicles of the Red Cross. We could see them. But it's obvious that they only got as far as the gate, which is where they stopped. And they confirmed this later, and in the Red Cross office on the left bank. On one occasion we also heard a guard saying something because certain things could be heard on the second floor, and the guard said, "Don't let them through the gate." They also came in October or -- I'm not sure whether it was October. In November and in December on two occasions. This visit probably had to do with the release of civilians in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, after December, 1993, when you were released from Heliodrom, did you have any contact with any representatives of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, since they had an office on the left bank of the Neretva River, in the eastern part of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about any contact that you had with them after you were released from Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it usually had to do with lists, with exchanges, and with searching for those who had gone missing. And in that office and in the corps office I saw next to my name that on all the lists they had compiled for persons they were searching for I saw that by my name it said "abroad." And elsewhere it said Juka had taken them away or it contained a reference to being abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, did you ever receive any documentation from the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I was registered in May, 1993, on the 25th of May, I received a little booklet with a number, first and last name, and the date. And when I left the camp, I received a certificate that I had asked for in that office, from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just like to point out something that's missing in the transcript. It's obviously a translation error. When the witness mentioned Juka took them away, she said it refers to the young men from -- from Vranka, from Vranka. The transcript doesn't convey this correctly, so could this please be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, you can continue. The last thing that's recorded in the transcript is that you received a certificate that you'd asked for in the office, from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the assistance of the Registry, I'd ask the witness be shown the document marked as P8774. For the transcript, that's 8774.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Drljevic, can you see the document before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What is --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a certificate which I have in my possession at home. And my father has this kind of certificate as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Is this the certificate you were just referring to that you received from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ma'am, do you know or did you have any awareness during the time period that you were in Heliodrom as to who the commander of that location was during the time period that you were there?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The camp commander -- or it was of the central military investigation prison, and that was Stanko Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many personnel were working in the Heliodrom building that you were detained in?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't give you an exact figure, because the room that we were in, three or four soldiers would come by. So I assume that that was the same for all the rooms. They worked shifts. But I can't tell you the numbers of the police establishment, because the security was supplied by the military police of the HVO, a unit whose commander was Ante Smiljanic. And I don't know how many buildings there were, so I really can't talk about numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, you told us earlier that you were released on the 17th of December, 1993, and can you tell us approximately how many other people, if any, were released on the same day that you were released?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such people, but I don't know how many. And I'm sure you'll -- you would be able to get those facts from the Exchange Commission and also from the authorities. But at any rate, many people were released. And I was actually surprised when I found that there were so many detainees on that day. But I think that even more people stayed on in the camp, more than those who were released. But as I say, I really can't speak about numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the assistance of the Registrar, I'd ask that the witness be shown the document marked 6955.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, do you see a document before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see your name on that document?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under number 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you recognise any of the other names on this document?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I recognise them all except, well, number 10, Zulka. That might have been her real name, but she's known as Fata. Or perhaps she has two names; I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, I'd ask that the witness be shown P5107, or the document marked -- previously marked as P5107.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, do you see a document before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see your name on this document?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Number 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, do you recognise any of the other names on this document?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I recognise Zulka again. I know her under the name of Fata. And I now see number 20, Ana Vejsil Orhan. And that confirms it. I assumed she was a Muslim that had converted, but I see it all here now. She married -- well, her husband was also incarcerated in a solitary confinement cell whether for having taken out some money or whatever, but his name was Ante. But she did that before she arrived in the camp. Yes, it says 1977. That means that she was 16 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, I just have a few more questions for you this morning. From the attic window of the room you were detained, could you see what was going on outside of the building?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you at any point in time -- or did you at any point in time see any of the other people that were detained in that building outside of the building?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Especially around the 30th of June, the 1st of July, up until the 5th. From the 1st to the 5th of July, actually, both day and night. In front of the building, in the playground, they would line up enormous columns. Hundreds and hundreds of people were lined up there. The buses would arrive. They would come down the Varda in a sort of column almost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me interrupt you there, ma'am. When you say "hundreds and hundreds of people were lined up there," can you tell us if you know who these people were?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know now that they were mostly people who were taken prisoner in their apartments in the western part of town or on the streets. Also, from the window we could see when the men from the rooms below were taken outside to air the blankets, and they would cover them with some powder because lice had appeared. They had lice in their hair. So they would use some powder for that. I could often see, in an open truck, people being driven off. Later on they told me, because I happened to recognise some of them and they recognised me, that they were going to do some labour, to do work. I saw that, and it remained in my mind because for a time -- well, I can't say every morning because it would stop for a few days. And then they explained to me that some would stay doing that work for several days. But very often, I would see a cistern truck with a square -- well, there was a sort of silvery grey square type of metal thing at the back. It almost looked like stainless steel, with a red cabin on it. I was very surprised to see this, because the driver was a man who lived in my neighbourhood. His name was Dragan Kozo [as interpreted]. Otherwise, he was in the military police. Kozul is his name. And the other man was his brother Stojan, and he was a cook at the Vranica headquarters. And that particular night -- and he also lived in Vranica. And that particular night, that is to say between the 9th and 10th of May, I would often say to the young guys to go to his flat and ask him to come down to the basement, but quite obviously he had another role to play. I also saw a truck or, rather, I saw it a number of times, but when I said that there was abuse, then I'm mentioning it in that connection. There was -- there were some tulips in different colours painted on a casket, and this was a truck that was used. People would come out slowly, and I noticed that they were stumbling as they were coming down off the truck and that they had their hands behind their backs, so that I assumed that their hands were tied behind their backs. And in front of them there was a soldier. A soldier stood in front of them, and he was shouting. He said, "Don't look at me. Look in front of you." That's what he was shouting to the people. And I recognised the voice of Ante Buhovac. It was dusk, so I didn't see him, but I recognised him by his voice. I couldn't see his face, but I recognised Ante Buhovac's voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, you'd like to ask you now about your health and the condition -- your medical condition at the time that you were released from Heliodrom. Can you please tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday during my testimony, I already said that that day, quite suddenly, I started bleeding when I was incarcerated in the MUP. And in -- I went to get help in the outpatients department, the clinic, and Dr. Ertan Kapetanovic was on duty working there, and I knew him from before, and he refused to give me any cotton wool or gauze or anything like that, so that this friend of mine gave me her daughter's nappies. In Ljubuski, when we arrived, all of us, we received a change of underclothes and stockings, socks, and -- well, there was this bleeding that continued for the next fortnight or so. Dr. Suko, whom I didn't know up until then, gave me Ergotil drops, and that stopped the bleeding. When we arrived at Heliodrom, I ate very poorly, just small quantities of food, so that Dr. Hadzic sent me to have a drip, an intravenous drip. And Ante Buhovac would do that a few times. Otherwise, his conduct towards me was very proper up until the time that I signed the piece of paper saying that I would go to the left bank. One evening he took me to the outpatients department, and I saw a tall person there. It was the HVO outpatients department, and it said Pehar on the doctor's coat. This was a surname I recognised as being a surname from Mostar. And I heard him talking to the ambulance driver, I assume it was. So that might have been July, because he said -- he was talking about how in this ambulance at the airport there were no -- not even bandages, let alone anything else. He mentioned, although I didn't know about this at the time, I didn't know what it was, but later on I asked around and got to know what this was about, he mentioned -- I'll paraphrase. He said, "What's this general talking about morale to us for and the successes at Boksevica when they slaughtered us like vermin?" Well, then I became really afraid, and I refused to go and have my intravenous drip administered. The doctor -- well, I concluded on the basis of what I had heard, I concluded that the doctor didn't know that I was actually a detainee there. Perhaps he thought that I was somebody working there or performing some sort of duty at Heliodrom. I'm not sure he realised I was a detainee. Dr. Hadzic was wearing a uniform, and over the uniform he wore a white doctor's coat. They said that he belonged to the 9th Battalion - that was the battalion that was put up in Jasenica - and that he was salaried, that he received a salary. But I must say his conduct towards me was very proper, and I even asked him for some sleeping tablets, which he gave me. I don't know what period of time that was, but I found it more and more difficult psychologically to take it all, so that in -- at one point, day, night, I had terrible hallucinations. I lost the use of my limbs. I became rigid for a time, and they said -- they called the doctor. Dr. Stranjak came with two male nurses, Seno and Omer, and I know them, I know them to this day. They live and work in the hospital, unfortunately. Dr. Stranjak was about 45 years old. He was a doctor who was a detainee, a prisoner, and he died of a heart infarction last year. During that period, well, I don't know whether from the tablets that he gave me, the sleeping pills, or because of my very poor psychological state, I imagined -- nobody told me, perhaps I dreamt it. And from this point in time, of course it all seems abnormal. I thought that my mother had died, that my little girl was ill, that my brother-in-law had been killed, and things like that. And under such circumstances, I wrote a letter. The woman that came with the Caritas organisation -- I wrote a letter to my sister to encourage her to persevere, to give her the strength to carry on. And I carried this letter with me all the time in my hand, and I hid it in my bra in case they were to search me. When Caritas came by, I went out into the hallway. The woman put her hands in my pocket, and I just dropped the letter, gave her the letter. Afterwards, she -- well, I just managed to write my friend's telephone number. I have a friend who lives in Rome. They got into contact with her, and they managed to find my parents and my sister, and they transferred them to Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Drljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I would propose we take our first recess at this point in time. I believe the examination-in-chief is complete. I just would like an opportunity to review my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you have completed your examination-in-chief, if I understood you properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, I would just like to consult with my colleagues and review my notes. I believe we are completed with the examination-in-chief, but I'd just like the opportunity to discuss that with the rest of my team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is now twenty-five past ten. We shall resume at quarter to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we have resumed our hearing, for the umpteenth time I'm turning towards Mr. Mundis to ask him if he has completed his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has indeed completed its examination-in-chief. I would ask for some guidance on when you would like us to tender documents into evidence, whether that would be at this point or whether you would prefer to wait until the complete end of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may ask to have them tendered right now, you may wait for the cross-examination to be finished; it's for you to decide. It's for you to assess. You may do it now or you may do it later. It's as you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Then just to avoid any confusion later, we would tender into evidence the following documents that were shown to the witness: 5107, 6955, 8774, those all being numbers from the Prosecution's 65 ter list. And it is the Prosecution's understanding that the capture of the photograph that the witness marked, that is IC0001, is already in evidence, but we would ask that be confirmed. I see Mr. Registrar shaking his head in the affirmative, but those would be the exhibits that we would ask to be admitted through this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of the procedure in the future, I think it would be good if the Prosecution, or the side calling a witness, after documents have been presented or after the conclusion of the cross-examination, I think it would be best if the party concerned state which document will be tendered into evidence, which document will be an exhibit, because if a document hasn't been tendered into evidence in the course of the cross-examination, we don't have to interrogate the witness in the course of our cross-examination. So if a document is tendered into evidence, we'll know that it's necessary to cross-examine the witness on the basis of that document. I think this should be done before the cross-examination is conducted. And as soon as one of the sides presents a document to a witness, I think that that side should state whether they intend to tender the document concerned into evidence, and this would facilitate the procedure for everyone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think Mr. Mundis has met your requirements. He has asked for three documents to be tendered into evidence. Those documents have been shown to the witness; therefore -- therefore, those documents, 5107, 6955, 8774 are thus tendered into evidence. Before moving on to the cross-examination, I would like to state that the Prosecution has dedicated 282 minutes to its examination-in-chief, so overall the Defence has 282 minutes. I'm turning to all of you, and I would like to give you the floor now. Who is going to begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. I will begin, and I will try to be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, madam. My name is Michael Karnavas. I represent Jadranko Prlic. I would like to begin by asking you some basic information regarding your background. We can get that out of the way and then we'll go into the substance of your testimony. Now, you've indicated to us yesterday and again today that you were a soldier, or in the military; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So at the time, at the time that you were arrested or captured, you were a soldier?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... when you were taken to Ljubuski and then later on to the Heliodrom, you were taken there as a captured soldier; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, before leaving the Vranica building, you had changed your clothes into a civilian; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not just you but others as well?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I remember yesterday, there was a gentleman there who I believe you said is deceased now, used to be an architect, that was on a megaphone, informing everybody on the outside that everyone inside were civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the whole purpose for changing --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I apologise. He mentioned this in connection to those he had negotiated with. When you said "everyone," were you referring to us inside or those who were outside?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me take it -- perhaps I inartfully phrased the question. Inside the Vranica building, which was the headquarters of the HVO -- of the ABiH at the time, there were soldiers in there, including yourself; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Many of them, including yourself, changed your uniforms in order to disguise yourselves as civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But I should point out that in my earlier statements, and I have said this in my testimony here, the main reason for which I changed into civilian clothes is that I started bleeding all of a sudden that morning, and I didn't have what I needed to stop the bleeding or to deal with the situation. But it is a fact that many of the soldiers did put on civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, if I remember your testimony yesterday, you were urged to change your clothes in order to disguise yourselves as civilians. So it had nothing to do with the bleeding. In other words, you were urged to do so.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when the gentleman was --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Than didn't apply to me, only to the men. Before we forced our way into the other part where the civilians were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. For the men soldiers it applied. In other words, they were trying to disguise themselves as being innocent civilians as opposed to being armed soldiers there on the west bank, in the heart of Mostar, in the headquarters of the ABiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see how that changes anything. If they were in uniform, they would have probably ended up in some sort of a pit like the other 13 young men who perhaps even changed into civilian clothes and then subsequently put uniforms on, because the wife of one of them said that the person shown in the photograph or in the -- in the film didn't have his jump -- it wasn't his jumper, that was just a way of saving their lives. I never concealed the fact that I was an army member, so regardless of whether I was wearing civilian clothes or a uniform, I would always say that I was an army member.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is yes. I mean, just to put it bluntly.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now -- and I don't mean to be aggressive, but questions are very, very specific and we can get along very quickly and have you back to Mostar. Now, when you were -- when -- you want to make a statement or you want to ask a question?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your leave, I'd like to say that if they changed their clothes it doesn't mean that they wanted to pretend to be innocent civilians. All they were trying to do was to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you -- when you were -- when you were imprisoned, you were imprisoned as a soldier; right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, before coming here today, did you happen to review your statements?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When was the last time that you read your statements?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I made the statements. Well, I can't remember whether the first statement was given in the department for investigating crimes in 1998 and 1999. And then there was the other one with the investigator -- or given to the investigator. I think that was in the year 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when was the last time that you actually read the statements? Not made them but read them.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the course of the proofing, two days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- so you're familiar with what you said back in 1998 and what you said -- I believe it was 2001. Let me check the date to be -- 2001. There were several interviews, I take it, back then. 2001 and 2002.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if one were to read these two statements, would they not walk away with the impression that by and large you were treated correctly while you were a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could say that that is correct given that no one beat me, no one raped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So that --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But given the conditions in the camp and the time, the length of time spent in the camp, I wouldn't say that I was treated correctly. If you take into consideration how this affected me, how I reacted to the situation, well, as I have already said, this is something I told to one of the investigators, after such a difficult experience, I'm glad that I don't feel any hatred. If someone now gave me the possibility of taking my revenge on these people, I mean if I could imprison them, prevent them from eating good food, prevent them from leaving the premises, I know I wouldn't be able to act in such a way. All I know is that those who are guilty or, rather, those who decided to treat people as monkeys and put them behind bars, well, if the people responsible for this attitude aren't the people who actually carried out the orders, those who devised the plan could be held responsible, and I think the Court should be held responsible -- should -- should determine their identity. Smiljanic was a commander, and he --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could interrupt here and if I could get you to focus on my question, because you had plenty of time on direct examination to tell us all about your experience. So --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- it's fact -- it's a fact, when reading your statements, back in 1998 when you were questioned by your own people and then when you were

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: treated correctly both in Ljubuski and in -- at the Heliodrom while you were a prisoner as a soldier; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean physical maltreatment when you used the word "maltreatment." But if someone spends eight months in a camp and no reason is given for this, I don't think it's normal situation.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right. And there's nothing in your statement, either back in 1998 or the 2001, where you talk about the psychological impact that you talked to us today. We won't find that in those statements, would we? Other than perhaps you didn't like the food because of the plates that were being used.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something I only found in the documents a while ago, but I found a certificate I was provided with by Dr. Hadzic. It's not dated, and it says that because of my general psychological and physical condition, I should be provided with a little more food, an additional ration of food. This is something I mentioned to the Prosecution. I went to be treated by a doctor who takes care of my mother, because after the film Grbavica I was really under a lot of pressure. I was really very stressed.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's talk about Dr. Hadzic. You did mention in your statement that you were treated by him. In fact, because apparently you weren't eating, that you were given a blood infusion; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right. And there's nothing in your statement that there was some sort of a quid pro quo, that you had to take these drips in order to go to be released, or sign some kind of document in order to -- that you had -- to get out. Because I understand in your direct this morning you mentioned something that you were given medical attention but there was a condition. Or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: I must be mistaken. Now -- now -- but in any event, there were no conditions. Dr. Hadzic gave you the blood transfusion, you got extra food, and they were looking after your health to the best that they could under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I lost so much weight that I only weighed -- I weighed 20 kilos less than usual, and then I had to be given this transfusion.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Yes. And my question is: Dr. Hadzic gave you the medical attention that you needed? All right.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Now, there's nothing in your statements, either the one in 1998, when things probably were fresher in your mind, than, say, the 2001, there is nothing in here about Caritas and you giving them a letter. Would that be a fair representation?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A while ago I received a tape from the woman, and --

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me. I'm asking whether in your statements -- My questions are rather specific. In the statements that you gave to your folks back in 1998, and in 2001, there's nothing in those statements about Caritas, is there?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's nothing about it. But no one informed me about the fact that I could only address matters that are referred to in the statement. I should then have been provided with the statement a lot earlier, not only two days ago.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'm sure the Prosecution will rectify that with other witnesses, but let me just ask you, when you gave your first statement, that was in a friendly environment, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: You were asked questions?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And you were -- they were there to help you. In other words, they wanted you to give them all the information that you possibly had; right? It's a yes or no. Or I'll take a maybe.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really say either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what I thought was most important, but my statement could be twice the length that it actually is. It's only now that I'm beginning to remember certain things, because I've always tried to leave this behind me, to forget about it all.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right. But in any event, they did not tell you, "We only have a limited amount of period --" Like we do say in this courtroom, we only have a limited amount of period to question you. They didn't say that to you. You were free to talk as long as you wanted; right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but as far as the second statement is concerned, the investigators had a limited amount of time -- or, rather, if -- if it takes three days to -- to make the statement, well, it was difficult for me to -- to carry on after -- after three days. It was too much for me.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we're going to go step-by-step, you know, "korak po korak." I'm sure you've heard that expression. Okay? Step-by-step. So let's stick with the first one: When you were talking to AID, your folks, back in 1998, friendly environment, you were not limited; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't limited.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And you were given the opportunity to read the statement and then sign it afterwards; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And then when you were questioned years later, well, perhaps the events were not quite as fresh in your mind, but nonetheless, you were

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: you were questioned on several different occasions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And again, they were pretty friendly folks?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: They weren't trying to intimidate you or in any way shorten whatever version you wanted to talk about, whatever topic, whatever issue; right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And of course they probably told you - as I'm sure they did - that if you remembered anything that you had forgotten to tell them, that you could contact them and tell them. Supplement, in other words, anything that you might have forgotten; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right. And when you came here to The Hague, you had an opportunity to read these statements again; right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And it would appear that some of the things that you said here today were not mentioned during the proofing session, during your conversation with the OTP prior to coming here; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's move on to another --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. For example, not yesterday, the day before yesterday, I said to the Prosecution that at one point in time I read about reading a movie, and it was right then at that moment that I remembered that the movie was called Escape from Alcatraz. Throughout all these years - and it's been, what, 13 years - it never occurred to me the name of the film.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Thank you. Now, I want to talk about your background a little bit. You're not a -- you don't have any military training, do you? Any formal military training.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And while you were with the army of BiH, you did not get any training from them either, I take it.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: They didn't send you off to some particular course for secretaries, because, as I understand, that's what --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Now, initially you got -- you got there, you started working with the Muslim forces before the formation of the army of BiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially, the 15th of April is celebrated as the army day, the 15th of April, 1992. I arrived about a month later. Now, as for the formulation, whether this was the Territorial Defence from prior to that, whether it was the reserve forces of the BH MUP from the September of 1991, it's hard to say.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right. But what -- I'm talking about before the formation of the ABiH. You were -- as I understand it, you volunteered. You started showing up.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And that was -- that was an all-Muslim unit?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly. For the most part. Since a large number of Serbs left town and a smaller number of them joined sometime in July of 1992. And also some Croats as well. But you also have to know that a large number of Muslims were engaged in the HVO. But let's say that, yes, for the most part they constituted a majority, the Bosniaks. They were the dominant ethnic group in the army units.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay. And again, we're going to go step-by-step. We're not going to miss any details. Now, at that -- at that time, you just show up and you're volunteering to sort of cook, make coffee, help out, do whatever you can because of the circumstances; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay. And then at some point you become a secretary.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was sometime in August of 1992, roughly. The unit was in the Luka barracks. It was billeted there. And I think that the first title was secretary of the barracks commander, and I remained there until January, February of 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right. And then you were -- then when you left that location, you still remained in that position as secretary?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secretary of the brigade commander. He was the same person. He was commander of the barracks in South Camp until November of 1992, and then starting in November of 1992 until he was killed, he was commander of the 1st Mostar Brigade. I myself didn't go to the Vranica building all the way up until February of 1993, because there wasn't enough space there. But I went every day to the barracks in South Camp.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right. But the answer again to my question is that you went there as a secretary and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And when we're talking about your commander, we're talking about -- well, he's get a nickname. Sometimes you refer to him by the nickname, sometimes you refer to him by his actual name. Hujdur. Hujdur, is that how you pronounce it?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mostly referred to him as Hujka. That's his nickname. But in order to make it easier for everybody to understand, I also use his official last name, which is Hujdur.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay. And his commander, as I understand it, was the head of the 4th Corps at some point; right? Arif Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Now, as I -- or correct me if I'm wrong, or help me out here: Would you as a secretary sit in on meetings when they were having discussions regarding operational matters? In other words, would you participate in those meetings?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Well, what about strategic or tactical? Did they consult you or were you part of the discussion group when these commanders were discussing these issues?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly, no. We would sometimes talk informally. If he wanted to tell me something he believed I should know, or if I asked something, but mostly I never asked anything. There was sufficient problems within the brigade that I had to deal with. My role was not a typical role of a secretary. I was more a go-between between the commander and the soldiers if somebody needed some assistance, if somebody needed to talk to somebody, had housing problems, or somebody was killed or wounded. So it wasn't a typical classical position as it exists in the military and as I later learned the position is. At any rate, I was not a typical secretary who was involved in things. I was definitely not a decision-maker.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right. Nor were you participating in certain discussions. Say, for instance, when they were going to draft an order, you weren't there, part of the discussions as to what should be put in the order, say, for some future activities?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And so if I were to, for instance, show you Arif Pasalic's order of 17 April, 1993, or Hujdur's order of, say, 19 April, 1993, where it would appear, at least, that some activity is being planned by the army of BiH against the HVO, you would not be able to assist us in interpreting these particular orders.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I would, since as I described in my statement, later on I had occasion, but I didn't analyse, study these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, once I left the camp, I wanted to see the order. I asked to see it. So information was available to me.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But as I said, this was an order that had been read, announced over the radio. Esad Humo, deputy commander who went to negotiate, also spoke about this order.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. When the order was drafted, I didn't see it at that time. It was strictly confidential, as they said. And I know that that evening it was sent via courier. I know that because I spent that night in Vranica. But I didn't see the order at the time back then.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right. Now -- but I just want to make sure that I understand. You did not participate in the drafting of the order or the discussions leading up to the drafting of this particular order; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This order was drafted at the operations headquarters of the brigade. It was under seal, and it was sent via courier. Naturally, later on we discussed it, all of us. I mentioned this yesterday. After the conversation with Mr. Pero Zelenika, Esad Humo said that he had taken a copy of the order out and showed it to him. So he was really angry about him getting that order. So what I knew was that this was a strictly confidential order.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And, in fact, you had indicated in one of your statements that after it was read it was supposed to be destroyed; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... didn't see this order?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when we say "at the time," did you see the order prior to -- to March -- to May 9th? If it was supposed to be strictly confidential, did you see it?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it then either. I saw it later, when I left the camp and went to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay. When you left the camp. In other words, you saw it after you left the Heliodrom, after you were released? Okay.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And just to be sure, just to save some time, earlier you indicated that you had no military experience and no military training as such, so would it be unkind of me to suggest that perhaps you're not the best possible person to give any meaning or interpretation to these particular orders?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. It could be said so. I think that there are witnesses who took part in drafting of the order. Unfortunately, none of the signatories are alive, none of the two of them. However, people who did take part in drafting, distribution, sending it out and so on, it is possible that there are people --

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: You're not one of them.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- who could say something more and something specific about one order or the other one.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: But you're not one of those people. I guess that's what I want to nail down. I want to make sure that I'm not foregoing the opportunity, for instance, to -- eliciting information from you regarding what exactly they intended when they talked about attacking HVO. So I want to be fair.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's say that you will find people more competent --

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Now, does that mean --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- who will be able to clarify this for you.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Now, in light -- in light of your experience and background, and given your tasks at the time, would that also apply to other matters, such as yesterday you were suggesting that it was the army of BiH that was doing all the fighting while the HVO was moving away and shirking their responsibility, and that was the reason, or one of the reasons, for the tensions?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I corrected that in relation to period of time from the crossing of the Neretva River up until approximately early July when the army members went to the positions in Podvelezje. And the weapons were taken by the HVO units either to the North Camp or somewhere in westerly direction. I know that at that time Commander Hujdur was angry. He spoke about that every time when they went to the positions in Podvelezje, a kilometre would be missing. Somebody with military training who visited these positions would be better placed to tell you about this, not I. As well as the air attack on the 9th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. So I take it you -- you want to correct yourself a little bit, if I understand you. And I'm not trying to suggest anything, but correct me if I'm wrong: If -- what I'm hearing is you're not competent or qualified to testify about certain matters such as to what extent the HVO was doing the fighting during that period of time when the aggressors - as you call them, the Chetniks - were involved in that area.
