utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say that I'm not sufficiently qualified, but that doesn't mean that I didn't know some things. Some things were known even to civilians who were there and who had nothing to do with the military. I hope that the Prosecution will use this opportunity and find people who are more qualified and competent to testify about the military issues.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Let's hope so. Now, you're also not qualified or competent to testify about how much -- the amount of weapons that were coming in in order to assist the Muslims at the time and where those weapons were coming from. You're not the best person for that, are you?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: In fact - correct me if I'm wrong, help me out here a little bit - yesterday as I was listening to you it appeared that almost all of your testimony, or at a great deal of it at least, with respect to those areas, the weapons, who was doing the fighting, the conflict, all of that was based on second or third or fourthhand information that you had received.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say that that's correct, but I don't know what you mean by third or fourthhand or fifthhand information.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Well, let's start with you personally did not observe it. That's for sure; right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: So you would have heard some of this information from the streets or the gossip and innuendo; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say that in the unit where I was, I stayed there the whole day, in the barracks, literally from morning to evening. So the information could have come only from soldiers, and then later on in Vranica, except that I wasn't in Vranica on Sundays. I didn't have much contact with people who were outside of this structure.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right. So you were getting your information from outside; correct? Okay.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: So that's why yesterday, quite rightly, you were very clear in saying that these are the things that you heard.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: So today, as you're testifying, you cannot -- you cannot assert with any degree of certainty what is fact, actual fact, what is confabulation or fiction, or embellishment, whatever that may -- or whatever else.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay. So as you sit here today and you're testifying, since the information you were receiving were from others, you don't know the -- how good the quality of that information was. You don't know whether it was truthful, whether it was partially truthful, whether it was an embellishment, whether it was totally false. You don't know. You cannot tell us today under oath. That's what I'm suggesting. And I'm not trying to be unkind, incidentally, I'm just stating a fact.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say that partially I will agree with you, because I personally didn't see this. One can claim with certainty only something one personally saw, experienced, felt, and I think that this is why I'm here today, to tell you about my personal experience.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Right. But your personal experience wasn't that you -- when you were describing, for instance, the tension between the ABiH and the HVO, that it was due in part because the Croat soldiers would not hold the line and it was up to the Muslim soldiers to do the fighting, that was not based on your personal observation. It's a yes or no. There's no in between. You either saw it or you didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it, but I couldn't say either that Croatian soldiers didn't fight. One could feel that they were leaving positions, the HVO. I heard about that. I heard that three shifts stayed back.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right. And could you tell us exactly the numbers of the HVO soldiers versus the numbers of the ABiH or, before that, the Independent Mostar Battalion that you were a member of? Could you tell us the relations, you know, in size, that is? Do you actually know? If you don't know, just say you don't know. Please don't guess.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when Mostar Battalion was established, it had 700 members. The HVO definitely was dominant in terms of numbers. However, this is information that can be provided to this Honourable Chamber through official channels.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right. And as I understand from one of your statements, you -- or even here today - yesterday - you had indicated that the HVO was better equipped; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And at some point, as I understand it, you mentioned it yesterday, that there was an agreement on cooperation between the HVO and the army of BiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... coordinate their activities; right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right. Now, before I go on to one other subject, yesterday you mentioned - or it might have been today - that at some -- yesterday, that at some point you had an opportunity to take members of your family, I believe it was your sister's children, to a place called -- if I did -- Kastela. Am I pronouncing it right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Something like that. That's that region that's sort of above Split, that overlooks, that has that panoramic view of that wonderful Adriatic coast?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And that's in Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's in Croatia, and it has to do with my friends.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Right. But --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've been friends since the 1970s.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: My point is, though, in the middle of this -- this conflict or this war, Croatia is allowing you to bring in children which would amount to displaced persons or refugees, however you want to call them, bringing them there for safekeeping. In other words, you weren't stopped at the border and said, "No. Where are your visas? Where are your entry permits? How long are you going to stay?" You were allowed to bring them there to safety in Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I could have done this years earlier. And I'd been able to do this up until now. My first cousin also got married in Croatia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: My niece, interpreter's correction, also got married there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I have nothing against Croatia or Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: I never suggested that, and if I have, I apologise. But my point is that during this conflict, during this period, Croatia is allowing you to bring in children to Croatia as a safe harbour; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I would like to point out the fact that even if my relatives, my friends are concerned, well, it's still the State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And in fact, you weren't the only one. Hundreds, indeed thousands from Bosnia went there to find safe haven, to find a place where they could be protected and away from the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And those were probably the policies pursued, and that was probably an agreement reached between the Croatian and the Bosnian government. I don't dispute that. What is more, I believe that that was a very positive thing.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: It was indeed. Now, lastly, before I finish, I want to talk to you briefly about your employment in Ploce. That's where you began your testimony yesterday, and I believe it was December 31, 1991, where you began, where you had indicated that you were fired from your position but you received a dismissal letter three months or so later, end of March, beginning of April of 1992. Do you recall saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Now, Ploce, for those of us who might not know, is in Croatia as well, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Small -- small place.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Sort of a port?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A port.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And during that time, all hell was breaking loose in that area, was it not? In other words, there was heavy fighting.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And, of course, it's a ways you have to drive -- I would suspect, if you're living in Mostar, you'd have to drive to Ploce to get there every day, unless you're staying there. But correct me if I'm wrong: It would appear to me from your testimony, and having thought about it a little bit, that maybe you didn't turn up for work for a few months before you got the dismissal letter. Am I wrong in making that assumption?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're wrong. Perhaps I made a mistake yesterday for not going into the details. I worked as a representative of that company in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So it wasn't necessary for me to go to work every day. We had to reach agreements for producing leather goods. Sometimes we would buy, but we would sell more often than buy. We didn't have a plan as to the amount of goods we should sell, but of course it was in my interest and in the company's interest to sell as much as possible. We were in contact over the phone on a number of occasions. The situation changed. Ploce was shelled. They had less and less work, and it became dangerous to travel around Bosnia and Herzegovina. So as an example, I could mention the fact that a man that I had professional relations with from Veselin Maslesa company in Banja Luka and who had a branch office in Prnjavor appeared at the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was an SDS representative, Dragan Djuric. He had a huge beard. And when cooperating with him, especially in 1991 when he made certain comments, I noticed that he was acting in a way that I could not accept, that I did not consider to be normal. Ploce couldn't function as it usually functioned, and similarly, I couldn't sell and travel as I usually did, nor could I cooperate with certain individuals on occasion. I had less work during that period of time, that is true, and let's say that that is why I was dismissed and this had a retroactive effect, and what I said later on has to do with the association in Jelah and with the negotiations between Croatia and Herceg-Bosna government when they tried to solve the problem of the employees who had been dismissed during that period.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay. And I guess -- I just want to make sure that we're all clear. I want to be fair to Croatia. I want to be fair to Ploce. I want to be fair to you. You're not suggesting here today, at least from the answer I got, that you were dismissed because you were a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the information that this association has, most of the people who were dismissed at the time or almost a hundred per cent of them were Muslims or Serbs. I didn't see that decision, but they have a decision made by the Croatian government, according to which all those who don't live in Croatia should be dismissed. I wouldn't say all those who are not Croats. And those negotiations were held in order to provide those people with some form of compensation, because --

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- people from that association told me that they were somewhat surprised, given my name. They said that they didn't have a single Croat on their lists.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Of course you provided that list and that information to the Prosecutor when you met with them, so he could share it with us and the Honourable Members of the --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the list. I don't have the list, but I did provide the information, yes. I don't have -- what's it's called? I don't have the list, but hopefully I should be able to get hold of it at a later date.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Now, I just want to get back to your earlier answer now. You indicated that there's a war; right? There's a war going on. I'm just -- okay.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: You're not able to travel as you used to because of the conditions of the war, so you're obviously not able to function in your capacity. Not because you don't want to but because of the conditions; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Ploce is under attack; right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: You're also having some problems with some of the employees, including -- and they seem to be Serbs. Right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And correct me if I'm wrong, but yesterday you indicated that after receiving this dismissal letter, along with the dismissal letter is an offer for you to work as, and I quote what you said yesterday, "as an exclusive representative of the company"; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: So it wasn't that they fired you. You got this letter, but then they're saying you can be the exclusive representative of the company; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The decision to dismiss me was then nonsensical. If they were offering me the position of a representative, that means I performed my duties correctly. On the other hand, I'd like to remind you of the fact that, according to the laws in force in the former Yugoslavia, there was a probation period that lasted for three months when one first started working for a company, a trial period. I started working in 1981 [as interpreted]. After this trial period had expired, I was employed for an indefinite period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: I understand all of that.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, or perhaps fortunately, that was the case. But at the time, it wasn't possible to dismiss someone unless you were in a position to prove in court that you had made a serious mistake. According to my assignment, I didn't have a specific job description. So even if -- if would have been impossible to give me -- to -- to dismiss me in 1991 because I hadn't performed the duties I was supposed to perform according to my job description.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Right. Now, because I want to end fairly soon but I don't want to give up on this point, what I didn't hear from you, what I didn't hear from you is that you actually made an effort to take them up on their offer to make you the exclusive representative of the company and then they said no. In other words, you never made the effort to follow up on the offer; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... there's a translation problem. Let me make sure -- I'll break it down. You never, you never acted up on the offer that was made to you to become an exclusive representative of the company; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. Three days later, the war in Mostar broke out. The --

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: I didn't ask you --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- fuel tank exploded.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: I don't mean to interrupt. I'm asking you: Before, you told us it was nonsensical. Now you're telling me -- you're giving me a different story. And I don't mean to be aggressive, but I just want you to be frank and honest with the Court. You were made an offer and you didn't take up that offer. You made absolutely no efforts; correct? It's either a yes or it's a no.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't take up the offer, but there's a difference between being fully employed and being an exclusive representative. You have full employment, you pay tax, you have social security. If you're an exclusive representative, you don't have any of these benefits, especially not during wartime.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: There's also a war going on; right? There's also a war going on; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay. And the company can't employ everyone the way they used to employ during peacetime; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but others remained employed. But let me explain this. In many companies, the employees were not working but they had their security, their social security, paid from 1991 up until the end of the war, and they didn't work during that period.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: I understand. And that's because they had the waiting list; correct? They were put on the waiting list that goes back to the former Yugoslavia. I don't want to get into technical matters, but when factories were running slow, you would be placed on the waiting list, you would get 80 per cent or 70 per cent of your pay until there was full employment again; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay. [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, you're not right. Those who went to the other armies and then destroyed towns, et cetera, well, they continued to receive social security. I'm talking about Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know what the situation was in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: In any event, where you started yesterday, you wanted to leave the impression with this Tribunal that the country that was hosting the thousands of Muslims during the war, the country that was also providing weapons to the Muslims during the war, was also -- is also the country that fired you as a result of you being a Muslim. Isn't that the impression that you want to give us here today, in spite of all the other explanations that you've given us?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the impression I wanted to give you. Let's say perhaps I made a mistake because I didn't show the Prosecution all the relevant documents that would support this fact.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Very well. And perhaps it was just an irrelevant matter that didn't need to be raised to begin with but just took up a lot of our time.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I may do this according to the rules of the Tribunal, but I could provide you with the documents that will support my claim later on. I'm referring to this dismissal and the decision taken by the Croatian government. I haven't seen these documents, that's true, but I've been told that they do exist, and I think that there is a team of lawyers in Croatia who represent this group of people, and I think there are 10.000 of them who are registered at the moment. But it is believed that from 1991 to 1994 and 1995, well, between 60 and 100.000 employees were dismissed. And this is a problem that's being much discussed right now. And in my prior statements given to the Prosecution, I didn't mention the fact. I found out about this decision and the activities of the Bosnian and Croatian government only about two years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, ma'am. First I want to apologise if I in any way offended you. Secondly, I want to thank you on behalf of Dr. Jadranko Prlic for answering our questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, I have no further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We still have ten minutes left before having our lunch break. I shall give the floor to the other lawyers, other Defence counsel, but I would like to ask them not to ask the same questions again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I won't put the same questions to the witness. I'll attempt to be very brief, but I fear that ten minutes won't be sufficient for me, so when you believe that the time for the break has come, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Ms. Drljevic. My name is Senka Nozica. I know -- I represent Mr. Bruno Stojic. I have a few questions for you. Yesterday, in response to a question from the Prosecution, you described the Vranica building and the number of entrances that could be used for members of your brigade to enter the building, and there's something that I'm not quite clear about. Were any parts of the building also used by the 4th Corps as well as your brigade, or is it just one area you're talking about? Because you mentioned an entrance used by the 4th Corps and an entrance used by the 1st Mostar Brigade. So what I want to know is whether you're referring to one area.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is one area, but there was a sort of partition wall dividing the area in that office. Yes, it is one area, but there were two entrances. One room but two entrances.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you say "two entrances" -- well, you said there was an entrance used by the 4th Corps, and you said, "We used some other entrance at the other side." Was this other entrance at the other side?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, on the same side of the building but in the direction of the Stjepan Radic Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you tell me what the area in the Kluz part meant for you or for the 1st Mostar Brigade. You mentioned your logistics centre there.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's where the logistics command was located. The entrance was from Stejpan Radic Street, but there was an entrance through the tunnel below the building. There are two pillars, and then there's the tunnel, and then you have two columns positioned in this way. On the western side there is one entrance, and on the southern side from the Stejpan Radic Street there was also an entrance into the Kluz building.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that this was in fact where the logistics command was. Was there some sort of a warehouse there in which perhaps weapons were kept?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't think there was enough room there. So not a lot of weapons could be kept there. But I've never been in that room, so I really couldn't say what was kept inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please, could you tell me, on the 9th of May, 1993, did members of your 1st Mostar Brigade, or Corps, go to that warehouse in the course of the day to collect weapons; and how frequently did they do so, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the night?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, in the course of the night.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On two occasions they took one case. Since the MUP building is there, it's parallel to that building, so someone from the MUP building noticed them and opened fire. One of the young men's rifles was hidden. It was no longer possible to have access there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So they went there twice during the course of the night and the third time they weren't successful in doing so?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yesterday, you mentioned Mrs. Mirzet Rizvanovic, who was with you in the prison in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please, can you tell me whether she was a member of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she was. She worked in the finance department in the corps logistics section.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, you mentioned two individuals. You mentioned her and Mrs. Mirna. You said that they had left before you had all been registered by the International Red Cross. Could you tell me for how long Mirzeta Rizvanovic stayed there?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For about ten days perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said something very strange about her. You used a verb which I found strange. You said she withdrew or got out. She got her secretary out. I know what this word means, but how did she get out? What did you mean when you used that word? And I'm being warned to speak a little more slowly for the sake of the translation. I'll do that. How did she get out? Can you remember the circumstances under which she got out?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirna Picuka was the first one to get out, to leave. Her mother was a Croat, and her father a professor at the university. And someone came to collect her. It was Mladen Misic's secretary. She had red hair and was in uniform. That's what they said her name was, in any event, and she was between 45 and 50 years old. On that day or on the following day, that's when she came. I didn't see documents of any kind. I believe there may have been a document permitting Mirzeta Rizvanovic to be released from the prison. I know that there was a woman called Jagoda who was a Croat from Stolac. The fact that she was a Croat was obviously important. She was from Stolac, and she took her to her home.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I just want to confirm what you just said. Could we say that some individuals got them out but no official procedure was followed?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, you said that you received a change of clothes in the prison in -- in Ljubusko, and you got a new pair of socks. Who made this possible? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't that evening. We spent that evening in that room. When we woke up in the morning, Ante Prlic brought us these items.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, could we just repeat who he was in the prison.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his position was. I don't know whether he was the commander of the prison or the commander of the military police that provided security for the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's what you said yesterday. With regard to that stay there, did Mr. Prlic make it possible for you to go somewhere and have a shower, to wash yourself?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When he brought us that change of clothes, he took us -- he took Mirzet and myself to see Jagoda, into the place where Jagoda was. As for the other three girls, they were taken to a woman who used to work as a cleaning lady. And I knew her aunt. Her name was Nada, and she used to work in a shop in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You were taken there to take a shower; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we generally say that his attitude towards you in prison in Ljubuski was a proper one?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In view of your yesterday's testimony, can we say that the attitude, the conduct of others who worked in that prison, their attitude toward you was also correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me give you a detail. I don't know the name of this young man. He was tall and blonde. On the day I was released, he came there, and he was there at Heliodrom, and he said good-bye to me cordially.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to ask Your Honours to go into private session for some five minutes, because I would like to put some questions pertaining to personal details of some other inmates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are currently in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, while you were in the investigative prison in Heliodrom, central investigative prison, do you remember sending a letter to anyone else in late October, 1993, perhaps? I'm just asking whether you remember sending any letter to anyone; and if so, then to whom?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this: I remember writing to Mr. Bozic after this episode with my back. I asked to be enabled to have contact with my father. But let me tell you this: Two days ago, when the Prosecutor showed me that letter, it was only then that I remembered the other two letters I sent to Bozic and Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In addition to sending letters to Mr. Bozic and Mr. Pusic, did you write to anyone else? I'm now directing your memory and telling you that could have been in October, 1993. Do you remember anything like that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to that -- or, rather, I wasn't a smoker. We had no communication. I didn't go out, or that is to say I went very seldom outside of the building and, say, into the basement. I went out maybe only two or three times. I wrote a letter, putting down names of men whom I thought to be on the ground floor. I thought that they were on the ground floor. I wrote to them, saying that I was sad that the commander had been killed, that my mother had died, and that I wanted them to send me cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was any of those persons called Jelin, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me ask you directly: Did you write a letter to someone called Jelin, a gentleman under that name?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And finally, as for your employment, Mr. Karnavas cross-examined you thoroughly, but I would like to ask you this: Would you agree with me that your statement, the statement you uttered about almost all of those who were fired during wartime in Bosnia and Herzegovina had no interruption in their service years. Let me ask you this: Do you know that even now in Mostar and in all parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the federation, and also in Sarajevo, very frequently there are many cases brought in court by people who were fired in 1993 under the same or similar circumstances as you who had an interruption in their service years, and they were dismissed because they missed the war areas or, rather, their places of residence and their places of work? Are you familiar with that fact?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, kindly. I have no further questions. Thank you for your proper attitude and your proper answers. I'm thanking you on my behalf and on behalf of my client. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now twenty-five minutes past twelve. Due to the fact that the witness must get something to eat, and the lawyers are definitely entitled to have a rest, and we shall resume again at 1.25. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.28 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. Mr. Kovacic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. By your leave, Your Honours, before I turn to the witness I just have a comment to make. Several times in the course of the evidence both the witness and the Prosecution used such terms as "Bosnian government," "Bosnian state." I would like to say this: In view of various changes that occurred with that entity over the years, I suggest it would be good to use consistent terminology in this courtroom; namely, to state "the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina" or "the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Through the documents we started using a standard, referring to that country as BH, meaning BH state, BH government, and so on. So I think we need to be consistent here as well. It's a formal issue. There is a state called Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is not known as Bosnian state, Bosnian government, or anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is noted in terms of the legal significance of the terms. When the Prosecution mentions the government, it should say "the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Ms. Drljevic. I'm Defence counsel for the third accused, Mr. Slobodan Praljak. I'm representing him here with my team. Since questions were put to you earlier by my colleagues, I won't take much time. You heard today that we, the Defence counsel, have a certain amount of time allotted to us, and I would like to ask you, as much as possible, to give yes or no answers to my questions. I will try to be as direct as possible. And if you want to give any additional explanations, give us some kind of a sign and then that can be clarified in re-direct with the Prosecution. I would like to clarify now something in relation to your employment with this company in Ploce, which as I think you said was called Kartonplastika.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Kartonplastika.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On page 8, line 21, you are recorded as saying that you believe that the dismissal that you received was, in fact, unlawful.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, the headquarters of that company, Kartonplastika, was located in Ploce.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Ploce is located in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, at the time you're referring to in late 1991, Croatia was already an independent state for half a year, was no longer a part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you lived in a country which was called Bosnia and Herzegovina, and your employer had its headquarters in an independent state which was no longer part of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia but was, rather, a part of a new state; Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in 1991, Bosnia and Herzegovina did not exist as a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, Croatia has existed as an independent state since June of 1991. It seems that we have a misunderstanding here. You seem to imply that Bosnia was not independent yet.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So Bosnia was not independent yet. That's what you're trying to say. But your company was based in Croatia, and Croatia was independent at that time. It wasn't part of Yugoslavia any longer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So Yugoslav labour law was no longer applied in that country. Did you take that into account when giving this qualification? You gave it to us.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but that wasn't stated in my dismissal letter. In the previous six months, they should have then signed a new contract with me, a new labour contract if the country had indeed changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was up to the employer.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it wasn't up to me to know these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, you're presuming that or, rather, the presumption is that everybody has to be familiar with the laws that pertain to that. If you were an employee of that company in Ploce -- but let's leave that aside. What's important is that the law of the sovereign independent state of Croat was applied to your labour contract at that time. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What do you disagree with?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I was employed according to one system of laws, then once that system was changed, I should have been informed that now my employment contract was subject to the laws of another state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's your opinion; right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you a qualified lawyer?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you consult any qualified lawyers at the time?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, we submitted all of the pertinent documentation to a team of lawyers in Zagreb who believe that they have a case, that our complaints are legitimate, and also our claims. And there are consultations going on, both with the Croatian government and that of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. So is that case in progress or is it being prepared for trial?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is being currently prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So there is no judgement yet?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned an association here. You said that it numbers 100.000 members. All of these people were left without their jobs in various parts of the former Yugoslavia. Now, this association which deals with Croatian former employees, do you think that this association is mostly focused on the reasons for termination of employment? Is that your opinion?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We think that there are hundred thousand members in this association. This is an association that for the time being has 10.000 registered members, and this is data that we received three months ago. The association is called Association for Protection of Dismissed Workers in the Republic of Croatia. So it deals exclusively with employees who used to work for companies from the Republic of Croatia. If allowed, I will try to supply to the Prosecution the decision on my dismissal as well as the list of persons who are currently members of that association.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You said yourself that in relation to that association and its activities, there was a lot of write -- a lot of it was written about in the press recently.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Based on press reports, it is clear that the essential question raised by that association is the right to shares that employees might be entitled to, and these companies have, in the meantime, gone to a restructuring process.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Shares which the workers are entitled to based on the privatisation process, the privatisation that was conducted in the meantime, as well as their entitlement to 24 salaries that the company must pay out to employees who were fired or dismissed under certain circumstances. I don't know how the lawyers are going to put this claim forth. Probably it will be based on the decision of the government. In addition to this, I think that there are other claims, claims for compensation which was not paid out to these employees who worked for Croatian companies abroad. For example, in Iraq, in Libya.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Correct. So there are a lot of issues raised.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: A lot of legal issues, I would say.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And one of the dominant issues is who is supposed to benefit from this change that the companies have gone through, because this is no longer a socialist system but a system that has been transformed in the meantime. That's the key issue.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't comment upon that. I don't think that that's the sole issue. At the time, I joined the army without giving it much thought, so I did enter into employment after that. However, there are many people who were left in the street without any right to unemployment benefits. They have no social security or medical insurance. So there are a number of people who have certain claims based on their employment abroad with these companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Ms. Drljevic. It stems implicitly from your replies - and you can confirm this - that for months you were unable to go to your company in Ploce. Previously, you had to go there.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have to go to Ploce for my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. You also confirmed that you did not accept an offer to start working as an exclusive representative, and you explained your reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It wasn't quite clear to me. Based on what you said, it seems that you were not prepared to accept the risk of making enough money through your work, because you would be paid exclusively based on sales results, meaning that if you concluded a contract, you would be paid; if not, you wouldn't. Was that the essence?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wasn't the essence. The key was the war broke out. I wasn't able to leave Mostar any longer. The whole town was destroyed. Even in the part of the city where I lived and where there were companies that I had associated with prior to that, I was unable to communicate with them. Nobody did any work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. So due to these circumstances, you were unable to do any kind of work for your company, be it as a permanent employee or as an agent of your company; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Do you know how many employees of that company were fired on the 31st of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But despite of that, you said that Croats stayed working and Muslims were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that, I didn't mean primarily my company. I used the information provided by the association headquartered in Jelah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. So not your company. But you don't know what happened, who was dismissed. Was it just Muslims or Croats and everybody else?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I hope that I will be able to provide a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Which means that you hope that you will be able to get an answer to this question?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to turn to another topic. You spoke about the events in 1991, about how -- how the independent company was established.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The year might have been 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was the main purpose of the establishment of this independent company which you joined practically right from the outset?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that its main purpose was to organise a resistance against Serbian and Chetnik aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It was in 1992. I'm saying this just for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you say Serbian Chetnik aggression, do you agree that that includes both the JNA and local rebels, if I may call them that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The HVO had the same task.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And this company was active within the HVO.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the HVO in its entirety and the company had the same purpose; namely, to defend from the aggression carried out by the JNA and local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And this is how it was throughout the entire 1992?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Brigade and corps were also established, but that had to do with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt you, but I'm focusing on what I'm interested in now. You explained to us how the corps was established, how it strengthened over the time, and how later the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But please confirm this to me: The Muslims and Croats together under the HVO defended Mostar from the aggression carried out by the JNA and local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the strength and weapons in possession of the defenders of Mostar. Would you agree about this: In 1992, all the way up until the time when the corps was established, the HVO was the dominant force in Mostar. It had greater strength and better weapons than anyone else.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Even -- and that holds true even after the corps was established. Even then, the HVO was dominant in terms of its strength and equipment, in terms of materiel and other equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You said that later on and in late 1992 some incidents started taking place having to do with weapons. This is on page 16, line 24, of yesterday's transcript. Do you agree with this? Do you stand by your previous statement?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you cited as an example - at least, I interpreted this as an example - that in Bijelo Polje someone called Andric - this is on yesterday's transcript, page 17, line 14 - that Andric seized a convoy of weapons valued at 800.000 Deutschmark and that it was under the control of somebody from Capljina, Mirad --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirad Cupina. Mirad. M-i-r-a-d.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, please tell me, whose convoy was this? Mirad. This person that you mentioned, who was the owner of that convoy?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he came from Sarajevo, and I think that he did have -- rather, I think that it came from Sarajevo and that its owner was the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this convoy had been sent from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know this for a fact?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that this is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you have no direct knowledge about this.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only indirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that you only heard this?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, Ms. Drljevic, as a member of the army and as a general citizen, you knew - I'm sure you learnt about this - that the JNA, before the disintegration of Bosnia-Herzegovina and before the new state was established, in fact had collected up all the weapons of the Territorial Defence in Bosnia. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what direction the convoy came from, who the owner was, but I do know that it was sent to the corps, because Cupina, this man Cupina, was the assistant commander to Pasalic, or one of -- one of the experts for logistics in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly, the convoy had come from another direction, but to the best of my knowledge, indirectly, and talking to other people in the brigade, I learnt that it was captured in Bijelo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Do you have any more detailed information or, rather, do you know who seized the convoy? Who is this man Andric, or what institution? Whose army?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the commander of the 1st Battalion from Bijelo Polje. I think his name was Miro Andric, and his nickname was Car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This unit, did it belong to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you certain of that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, tell me, madam, please, did you hear or do you know anything about the fact that at that same time and before that and after that, that from Croatia a convoy of weaponry arrived intended for the entire defence against the JNA and the Serbs? That is to say intended for the army, for the volunteers, to begin with, and for the HVO. Do you know that? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that, but it might have come from Croatia and along the borders of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. But quite possibly there was a large number of those convoys coming in from -- or coming in to Bosnia-Herzegovina or exclusively paid for by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. But regardless of who paid for it, the fact remains that the convoy, with weapons both for the BH army and the HVO, came from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to show you a document by way of an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, may I have the usher show us document 3D0006.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The translation of the document is on the next page. In English, please. We have the next page. Would you, madam, take a look at the Croatian version. Ms. Drljevic, from the first line, under the word "Nalog," we see that this is for materiel for the requirements of the armed forces of BH Mostar. So this is one contingent, and we see that those responsible for taking over this material was Mr. Emir Beslagic and Seta Sujab. Now, the first question is this: Do you agree that these gentlemen who were supposed to take over the weapons have typically Muslim names?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And this other one was an active officer within the BH army. The army component in the army of the Federation. I don't know him personally but I do know that I saw some documents bearing his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. So it's quite clear from this document that the Croatian government, the Ministry of Defence in Croatia, is sending -- is sending weapons to the BH army. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to tender that document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, in the future - and I've said this already - when a party submits a document - I insist on this - I do want to have a paper copy, a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I thought that it was distributed. Now I discovered that it didn't. I would like to have usher to send the document. However, Your Honours, you will see here a little bit more documents. I will not draw all of them due to the fact that some facts are already established, and I don't want to do too much. I'd like to ask the registrar -- or the usher to place the second document on the screen now, please. May I have the Court's decision? Has the exhibit been admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to the first document, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would object on the grounds that there's no proper foundation for this document to be admitted through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you explain why the Defence failed to offer the proper foundation for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's no evidence that this witness had ever seen this document before or knew the contents of this document or knew who signed the document or any such proper foundation for this witness to be tendering -- for this document to come into evidence through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, respond to that. [Interpretation] In conformity with the instructions given by you a few days ago, especially with the revised version, I consider that we do have the possibility of showing the witness the document and then can tender it into evidence because it is linked to the topic of discussion. That's point one. And point two: In this specific case the witness recognised the name of one of the individuals who is mentioned in the document as the individual who will take over the shipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can I have a number, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It will be 3D0006. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for purposes of clarity, later on in our Defence case we shall, of course, have a large number of documents of this kind, and we shall indeed hand them over in a package, and an individual will be able to explain the origins of the documents. I would now like to show this witness a few more documents of the same type, and all of them refer to the period of time that she testified about. So we have another document dated 1992, and then four documents after that which take us up until March, 1993. And I'd like the usher, with the Court's permission, to display the documents on the monitor. 007 is the first document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to add that what I said a moment ago, that is to say that I know the name of the individual, but first of all Seta Sujab, I know him from after the war, that is to say professionally serving in the BH army. Of course I have never seen this particular document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I just want to show you several of these documents so that we can agree, you and I, that it is a fact that almost all the weaponry used both by the HVO and the BH army during 1992 and 1993 in Bosnia-Herzegovina came from Croatia. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree, but these are not documents that I had access to. But otherwise, yes, I do agree with your assessment. Regardless of where they came from, they had to pass through Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I won't be taking up more of your time by tendering six similar documents dated 1993. We will do this -- up to March 1993. We'll do this through various witnesses. And if this witness has confirmed them, then there is no reason for me to take up more court time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, let's move on. And if I might summarise, to speed up, from pages 19 and 20 of yesterday's transcript, yesterday's testimony, you said that especially as of January, 1993, and from that date onwards, that incidents began to take place between the HVO and the BH army. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we refer to Mostar, then I can say that there was increased tension, and there were more frequent instances where trucks were stopped, and there was resistance linked to an order -- I think it was an order of the 20th of January. 15th or 20th of January, 1993, according to which the BH army units should be resubordinated or, rather, placed completely under the command of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. You told us all that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'm now going to show you another document which indicates a somewhat different situation, and I'd like to hear your views.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the usher place the document 3D0012 -- 00012 on the screen, please. That's not the document, madam. It's another one. May we zoom in, please, so we can see the document properly. We also have a translation of the document, but I would like the witness to see it. That's my intention here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So, Ms. Drljevic, can you read this document out to yourself, please. Would you take a look at the signatory, the signature to this document in particular, please.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, from this document, according to the assessment made by the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the army of BiH, Sefer Halilovic, it would emerge that he considers that the situation in Mostar and relations between the command of the BH army units and the units and command of the HVO, is good, and I would even say fairly optimistic, judging by this letter. That's what this says, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think this was the result of negotiations that were held between Mr. Pasalic and Sulejman Budakovic, who was his deputy, and they had been in Prozor previously, paid a visit to Prozor and Jablanica. I think I remembered the date and that it was March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really -- or all I can say is that both sides invested efforts to calm tensions, because I don't think this situation suited anyone, an armed conflict. And when I say "armed conflict," now, I'm not fully competent to talk about that, but I think that even people who were in responsible positions did not expect a conflict of this kind to actually take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So bearing in mind what you've just told us, do you feel that the incidents that you mentioned were the result of somebody's wish, intention, desire, or anything of that nature, or were they simply the result of the situation and circumstances that existed? And I can call it quite simply chaos and an organised defence against the Chetniks and JNA that we saw at that time.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I followed your question. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. I wasn't clear enough, and the question was a long one. Let's break it up into parts. Do you consider that the incidents that you mentioned and that we talked about previously were the result -- or let me put it this way: Why did those incidents take place? Were they planned by anybody? Did anybody want them to happen, any institutions; the HVO, the BH army, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would -- it would be too much to expect of me, an answer like that and an assessment on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, the document that you have before you directly refers to the visit by Arif Pasalic, the commander of the 4th Corps of the BH army. You of course knew Pasalic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that was the person who was the commander of the 4th Corps with headquarters in Mostar; isn't that right? We talked about and we discussed him, did we not? It's the same Arif Pasalic that you yourself mentioned earlier on.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I'd like to tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can I have a number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D00012. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, now we saw this document, and we heard your description of this situation as it existed in early 1993. You yourself mentioned the events of the 19th and 20th of April and how the relations were tense. Is it true that by the 21st of April the tensions calmed down?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that these incidents that you mentioned - and we saw a document referring to them - that there would be an incident and then the situation would calm down and then there would be another incident and then another escalation of tensions? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have already described this joint commission which was housed in the water utility company. This commission toured the entire city. It was a mixed commission. I remember that at some location the vehicle of that commission was hit, but nobody was injured. So, yes, that was an additional incident. And what was especially troubling were the arrests of the army members in town. It went over a long period of time of one month. Most of the negotiations concerned the proper solution to that problem, to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think that we fully agree, Ms. Drljevic, concerning what you said. So it was mostly through the efforts of commands of both sides that they attempted to control the chaotic situation where incidents erupted even between allies. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see -- can we put to the witness the next document; 3D00016. [In English] 3D00016.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Drljevic, would you please take a look at this document. Check the signatories. My first question is: Did you see this document at the time?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you hear the announcement on -- through the media?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was this also one of the examples of the efforts invested by both sides to calm down the situation?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is precisely related to that joint commission. It's possible that instead of Redzo Mehic it was Fikret Krekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, but no matter.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you agree that the signatories on this document, Arif Pasalic and Petar Zelenika, were definitely persons who participated in this process?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, perhaps, as someone who lived in Mostar, as someone who moved in the circles of military commands of BH army units, do you remember whether this plan announced by this document was actually implemented?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you scroll up the document, please? It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it's the 21st of April.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Rather, I apologise. Were you going to say anything else?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A part of this pertains to the fact that facilities could be secured exclusively by the members of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the next topic, if I may point this out to you, and you can say whether you agree or not, is under "The distribution or allocation of certain military facilities"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Another detail in this document, under item 3. It says that -- and I think you mentioned this in your evidence. It says here that long barrels are hereby banned, or, rather, no one without official duties is allowed to carry long barrels. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but perhaps somebody from the commission should say more about this, because they would be better placed to explain this. It was impossible to implement this. We didn't have sufficient space in South Camp, and it wasn't practical for people leaving and going into shifts -- well, the problem was that most of them had to take their weapons home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'm sure we could discuss this question at length and debate it, but I wanted to hear from you, as somebody who was there at the time. You were a lady who lived there at the time. I wanted you therefore to confirm that incident erupted and that both sides took steps to eliminate them, to limit them, and to try to advance the -- the alliance.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And people who were involved in drafting this order and who are still alive would be better placed to tell you more about this. I just know that the vehicle of this commission was fired at. I know that it came to the Vranica building and that Damir Sipar conducted an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now confirm that there was a will to implement this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask the usher to put document D00017 up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, please take a look at the document, who signed it. I have just one question related to this document. And once you've taken a look, tell me, please, do you agree that this document reflects precisely what on the previous day, in the joint statement issued by Pasalic and Zelenika, was written; namely, this is confirmed here by the HVO commander Milenko Lasic. He's hereby issuing an order ordering his troops to act in accordance with what was announced on the previous day with that agreement.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure that there must be documents in the archives of the army which we could have provided to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that that is so, but I'm trying to clarify what I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask also that both of those documents would be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, there are two documents in this case. Could we please have a number for them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. These two documents will have numbers 3D00016, and 3D00017. Thank you, Your Honour. The documents have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, we will now turn to another topic. Yesterday, when asked by His Honour towards the end of day, on page 73, line 22, of the transcript, the Honourable Judge asked you about your ability to remember names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... private session. Then I will ask for a brief private session, just for two short questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back into open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, a few seconds ago, has just told us that he has concluded his cross-examination. I shall now turn to Madam Alaburic and ask her whether she would like to put any questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Drljevic, I'm Vesna Alaburic, attorney from Zagreb, and I'm Defence counsel of General Milivoj Petkovic, who is one of the accused in this case. You answered many questions today about your dismissal, but I'm going to ask you a number of additional questions because I think this will help us clarify matters. Today you told us that when Yugoslav laws, labour laws were in force, and I'm quoting you, it wasn't possible to dismiss anybody without proving in a court of law that he had made a serious mistake. That was recorded in today's transcript. The page was 54, line 23 and 24. Do you stand by that statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. May I just correct myself? It was very difficult to be dismissed once you were given employment without any time deadline.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. Thank you for your answer. Now, if I tell you that in the Republic of Croatia the first Croatian regulations and law, labour laws, were enacted in 1995, the first law, and that in 1991 we still had in force the republican labour law and the so-called federal law on the basic rights emanating from employment, that those were rules and regulations which were fully in force at the time when you received employment and at the time that you were dismissed as well, which was at the end of 1991, would you then agree with my observation that at the time when you were dismissed the regulations that were in force in the Republic of Croatia made it very difficult for anybody to be dismissed from their job?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But may I add that I, pursuant to a power of attorney, I received my work booklet in 1995 or 1996. I wasn't expecting to speak on this topic at greater length. Otherwise, I would have prepared myself for it and brought in documents to bear out what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We're just talking about rules and regulations at the time you received your dismissal letter. Now, from the reasons stated for your dismissal, which you described to us yesterday and which was recorded in transcript -- in the transcript on page 8, lines 13 to 15, it would emerge that you yourself were dismissed for reasons which were conditioned professionally by your job.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: After that, you told us that you were dismissed probably because a decision made by the Republic of Croatia by which anybody who did not have residence in Croatia had to be dismissed. Now, in that connection, I would just like us to clarify the first point. In the dismissal letter that you received, no mention is made, I assume, by a single word of the problem of your residence in Croatia or lack of residence in Croatia. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
