utterances.text: You told us today that the government decision that you referred to is one that you did not see yourself, and therefore I conclude that somebody told you of the existence of that government decision and explained what it contained.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us with certainty that it was indeed a decision by the Croatian government and not, for example, the law on employment governing foreigners?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure it was a government decision, a decision of the government of the Republic of Croatia. And I hope -- or, rather, I don't know what the procedure is in the law courts. Probably it was my mistake that I did not prepare myself better with respect to the documentation needed, but that the knowledge we had about negotiations between the two governments and the involvement of the legal team on my case, then I would have brought this in as material evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me when I say the following: That had in the Republic of Croatia a government decision actually existed which would have enabled workers who did not have residency in Croatia to be dismissed, would your employer then, in the dismissal letter, state as the reasons for a business -- business-related reason for your dismissal?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your dismissal letter and in the decision on dismissal, did it say that you did not have the right to appeal, that you did not have the right to take your employer to court, and that you did not have the right to appeal the decision of the dismissal?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really can't say. I didn't expect you to ask me questions like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us, then: You said that you did not challenge the dismissal at the time, the decision on dismissal, and you said that the day after the work broke out. Can you tell us whether it was the war circumstances that were truly the sole reason for which you did not contest the decision about the dismissal?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does this mean, in other words, that the reasons set out in the dismissal letter that you considered to be well-founded and that is why you did not have the intention to appeal them and to contest them?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I just analysed the situation a little later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm interested in. You said that two years ago, you learnt of the existence of an association dealing with the continuity of labour and employment for workers who had received dismissals at the beginning of the 1990s, and these employees were mostly Bosniaks and Serbs. Now, my question to you is this: Let's clarify whether that was actually the case. Did you learn about the existence of this association two years ago?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just by chance on television.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, your knowledge about this association, did it influence your position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honour. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, can you tell us whether you learnt about the existence of this association and the goals that the association was fighting for, did that influence your position regarding the dismissal letter you had received 12 years prior to that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, yes. However, I must say that I was very surprised that a decision of that kind had been made in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What decision?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that that government decision didn't exist, but this isn't the subject of our debate. Now, is it a fact that when you learnt about this association this influenced a change in attitude on your part and that, in giving your statement in 2001 and 2002, you briefly said that you had been dismissed when the war broke out because, and I quote, "I was not able to go to work." That is on page 3 of your statement. And today, you are, nevertheless, trying to present this dismissal in quite a different light.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, this is a question of terminology. I really did not go to work. I couldn't perform my work. We would have meetings three or four times in the firm itself, and I would go from time to time, but for the most part I worked in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and my job, my work, was linked to travelling round to visit the buyers. But once again, that would be going to work, come under the term of going to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All I want to say is that before you learnt about the existence of the association, you said that you were dismissed because you couldn't go to work, whereas now you're telling us something quite different. So that was the basic grounds for my question. Now, thank you for answering questions about your employment and so on. I'm not going to ask you any more about that, but I'd like to deal with the Vranica buildings and -- or building and what took place in that building on the 8th and 9th of May. You referred to a part of the building that you called the cellar, or basement, a few times, which is where the brigade had its headquarters and the corps had its headquarters. Can you tell us now, please, whether it was something that is generally considered to be the basement of a building, or was it a shelter that had been well organised with well-organised office premises and all the furnishings that that would imply?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the 9th and 10th of May. Well, yes, I was in Vranica on the 8th as well. But, yes, they were sales premises that had been properly furbished where the brigade was put up, and there was the leather factory from Visoko that had its premises there, and another company, the Vranica company.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you describe that basement or cellar to us, please. Were there several rooms in the basement?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were they properly painted? Was there furniture there? Did you have telephones and things like that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was the basement equipped as a shelter?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to a certain extent, yes, in view of the fact that it was a rather new building. Well, perhaps the building had been built ten years ago. But according to the law, you had to have a shelter in each newly constructed building, and that the shelter was to be in the basement. So it wasn't a basement for a boiler room or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you for describing the basement to us. Now, I'd like to refer to a statement you made yesterday in order to clarify it. You told us yesterday on transcript page 34, lines 8 and 9, that you were lacking ammunition in the 9th or 10th of May - in 1993, that is - and that it was becoming clear that you wouldn't be able to defend yourselves. Now, in that connection, I would like to clear up the following: It would appear that the BH army was shooting from the Vranica building, that it took part actively in the fighting from the actual premises of the Vranica building and the close vicinity of the building.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can we clarify the -- something with regard to the telephone lines in the Vranica cellar or, rather, the area where the BH army soldiers were located as were the residents of the building itself. You told us yesterday that for the whole time you had telephone communication with the forward command post in the building of the SDK, the social accounting services building, on the opposite bank of the river Neretva. And that statement was recorded on page 31 of the transcript, lines 24 and 25. So I'm now asking you to clarify. When you said the whole time, did you mean the whole 9th and 10th of May, 1993, or what? What period did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was radio communication which was encrypted. Encrypted messages.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you actually communicate with the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Via -- with the help of codes, encryption.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know how many messages were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I wasn't in the signals section the whole time.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, much less. Far fewer. Perhaps four or five. Four or five that I know about, but quite possibly there might have been 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you reproduce the contents of those statements, or messages, rather, that were exchanged? What were they about?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last one I received was, "Hold on, we're coming." And in one of the previous messages it was that, "We've reached the prison and the Rondo." And that was only partially true. I checked that out later on. One of those messages asked that anaesthesiologists be found, Dr. Milavic and Jakupovic. And this indicated most probably that there were wounded. And later on I learned that Dr. Milavic responded to the call-up but that Dr. Jakupovic stayed on the right bank. She stayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you also told us about communication with people from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you told us that somebody called up from the HVO - and that is recorded on page 33, lines 22 and 23 of the transcript - and you also told us that you called, or one of the gentlemen who were with you called Jadran Topic, and that statement is recorded on that same page in lines 15 and 16. Now, on the basis of those statements of yours, would I be right in concluding that your communication with the HVO throughout the whole time was unimpeded?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us this: Was the HVO -- had it wanted to, be able to interrupt the telecommunications from the area that you were in?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could have.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now a few questions about your leaving the Vranica building. You told us yesterday about how the wall was broken through - and that is recorded on pages 31, lines 8 and 9 of the transcript - and you also mentioned that this was proposed by some individuals who knew how the building had been built and knew that this was a partition wall made of bricks and that it could be knocked down. Now, tell us, did these same people know where the road was leading to once you had done away with the bricks and the wall?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since one of those individuals were there all the time, at the headquarters of the brigade all the time, whereas the other young man just happened to be there and he happened to work in Vranica before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But tell us, where did this other path lead to?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second entrance of the same building, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, of the same building. Can you explain to us why you had take down the bricks and with -- and then go to another entrance if you wanted to get out to the second entrance and not to the first entrance that was closer to you? Was the reason perhaps this - and I apologise if my conclusion is wrong: Was it because that at the second entrance you could introduce yourselves as civilians to the people who were waiting for you rather than going through the first entrance that was the entrance used by the brigade and corps command? I think that would be quite understandable. You wanted to try and save yourselves.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never thought about it in that way. I didn't know whether there was someone with weapons on that other entrance, perhaps, at that other entrance. So I personally can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So in fact, you broke down a wall, you shot at a door without knowing why you were actually doing that.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know where we were going. Now, whether the people who knew this was a partition wall knew where it led to -- perhaps they did, because there was once again a basement premises, and then you would go up along a second staircase, but I really can't say. But I do know that the entrances where the soldiers were standing, there was absolutely no chance of us leaving that way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As for changing the clothes, you said that you were in uniforms and then you changed your clothes. Was it after you had broken down the wall, when you were close to the second entrance, or was that before, when you still didn't know that you would get basically just to the same entrance of -- to the second entrance of the same building?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I changed in the first entrance, after I woke up. I don't know for the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you change into your own clothes or into somebody else's clothes?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I changed into the clothes of my friend, my lady friend where I had spent the previous night.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions concerning the Vranica building. Thank you for your answers. But I would just like to put other questions to you concerning military operations, even though, when asked by Mr. Prlic's counsel, you said you were not an expert for military issues, but I'm still going to press you for another explanation. Yesterday, you mentioned an operation called Bura in November of 1992.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you said how the army of BH tried to attack the Chetniks and that the HVO was quite passive about it. I'm now paraphrasing your words. You said this on page 18, lines 10 to 24. I would like to ask you this now: Do you know that the Operation Bura was supposed to cover a much greater area than Podvelezje which you mentioned? Did you know that it also included Stolac and a much broader area around Mostar? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. Mr. Jonjic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will attempt to tender into evidence some 10 to 12 documents through this witness. We have copies prepared for all Judges, and I would like to ask the usher's assistance in order to distribute them. I hope that there will be no problems with e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Drljevic, good afternoon. My name is Tomislav Jonjic. I will be putting questions to you on behalf of Mr. Coric. Since my colleagues exhausted quite a number of questions that I was going to put to you myself, and since you said you had no military expertise, I will try to limit myself to the topics which in my view you should be familiar with. Tell me, please, you spent your whole life, or most of your life, in Mostar; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Based on your yesterday's evidence, page 9, lines 16 to 18, you said that the war in Mostar broke out in September of 1991. On the 19th of September, 1991, when the reservists of the JNA came into town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Since you spent your whole life in Mostar, and since you were quite active in the circles from which later on the BH army was founded, can you tell us, what was the reaction of the SDA or, rather, the Bosniak Muslim residents once the reservists came into town?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I was never a member of the SDA. I can't speak on behalf of the general public. I came into conflict mostly with my friends, Serbs that I used to socialise with, especially since I lived in the vicinity of the South Camp where the reservists were billeted. I personally was upset with their status, and I even stopped seeing some people when I realised that they supported that, but I can't say about other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar whether there were any demonstrations? Were there any public expressions of revolt on behalf of the Muslim residents?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think there was. What I know I learned later. I know several men who had been engaged in the reserve forces of MUP and who patrolled in the part of town where I live. Later on, I was upset by the fact that the first conflict and first incidents took place precisely there while on the other bank of the Neretva life went on as normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You know the ethnic composition of Mostar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you know the ratio between Croat and Muslim residents in Mostar in 1991 in percentages?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You don't know percentages?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the difference was 1 or 2 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You say that from the very beginning you were in the Independent Company which later grew into Independent Battalion and then that became the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: My colleagues asked you about the difference in strength between the members of the HVO and the army of BH. Can you give us some reasons, can you give us your interpretation for that situation where in one city there is an equal number of Muslim and Croat residents, and initially there was just one company and one brigade of the BH army, whereas there were nine battalions of the HVO simultaneously, at the same time?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't go into reasons for that, but you have to bear in mind that the war in Croatia had started significantly earlier. So the HVO had huge support and assistance from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said several times, both yesterday and today, that in the course of 1992, especially up until November of 1992 when the 4th Corps was established, the company and, later on, the Independent Battalion were within the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the time.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. But for a part of the year the documents referred to this fact, and I said so previously. We used terms "commander" and "command," Croatian terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So in the operation sense they were under the HVO.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a certain extent. I don't know until what time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: On page 10, lines 5 to 7, of the transcript yesterday, you said that your father had been imprisoned and taken to the Chetnik camp in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: On page 59 and 60 of the transcript, you said that he had been exchanged there and went back home. Do you know where this exchange took place?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Stolac. But they were released in Berkovici, and then they had to walk for seven kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You, at that time, which was August of 1992, were already in the command of the brigade. Was it already the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I remained in the barracks, South Camp barracks. My father was exchanged in July, and I went looking for him before that, when the first exchange took place in Ljubuski, and it was only then that I had learned that my father was in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you know who agreed this exchange? Was it agreed or negotiated by the BH army or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Were you present at the location where the exchange took place?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. In Ljubuski I saw a lot of people. A woman told me that my father had been taken out as though to be released, and then he came two or three days later. Quite accidentally, I stood there outside. I saw a bus pass by, and accidentally I went home and I found him there in prison clothes. I know that in Metkovici he gave a statement for television, and he said that we shouldn't forget that people had remained behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now 3.00. We must have a technical break, and we shall resume at twenty minutes past three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. We are going to work, at most, another one hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before we continue, I would like to bring to your attention an error in the transcript, which could be a result of me speaking too fast. On page 106, line 16, instead of "the company," it should say "one battalion of the BH army and nine battalions of the HVO."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Madam, now let us go back to what we were discussing. Were you personally present when your father was exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: But I assume that you talked about the conditions prevailing in the Chetnik camp, about people who were imprisoned there.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you what municipalities the people who were in the camp were? Were those mostly people from Eastern Herzegovina, from the eastern bank of the Neretva?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you something about the ethnic make-up of the people who were detained and then exchanged in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did speak about that. I remember that those were mostly Muslims, and then some were Croats from Kocina Opina neighbourhood or, rather, from Gnojnica and Bijelo Polje. Yesterday I gave the names, or, rather, he gave the names of people who had been in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: But those were mostly Muslims.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: The HVO handed over to the JNA captured JNA members and members of the Chetnik formations, and in return, they got mostly Muslims. Do you know where these people were housed once -- because the areas where they lived were mostly still occupied. So where did they go to live once they had been exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went back mostly to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, on page 59 and 60 of the transcript, you said that your father was among those who returned to an office led by -- he went to an office led by Miroslav Bosnjak. Even though his last name is Bosnjak, the man's a Croat. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. And I find it sad that people are described by their ethnic origin. I know that his last name was Bosnjak, and I know that Croatian chequerboard was in the coat of arms, and this was the office for victims of Chetnik terror. That's what it was called. I don't know what you're aiming at.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: It was an office of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but my father was a civilian, as were many other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may ask for usher's assistance, please show us document 5D01011.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that we have some difficulties with the e-court. I have sufficient number of hard copies. I can even provide one to the witness, with the Court's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if the e-court fails to work, we can have the documents in the hard copy on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know how to ensure that everyone, including the Prosecution, has the relevant document. I don't know what the technical procedure would be. We seem to have the translation on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, is this office that we have been discussing the one contacted by your father and led by Mr. Miroslav Bosnjak, the lawyer?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. However, I would like to point out that on a number of occasions I also went to that office. There was a fair-haired young man, I don't know what his name is, but his father used to work with my father in the tobacco factory. I can't remember his name, though. When I told him that my father had arrived, they contacted him themselves, and I believe that he provided them with the names of about a hundred Croats who had been detained. This is something I mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: If we have a look at this document -- it's not necessary to read through the entire document, but if we have a look at the document, we can see that it has to do with the municipal office of the HVO in Mostar. They're contacting -- contacting the Red Crescent in Mostar, which is a humanitarian organisation, and they're informing them of the fact that, over the last three and a half months, because it says that the office was opened on the 9th of June, 1992, and this submission is dated the 28th of October, 1992, so it says that the office was involved in an exchange of prisoners from Herzegovina when 800 persons were liberated, mostly people from Eastern Herzegovina. So we agree that this is the office contacted by your father. And now let's have a look at a document that has the following number: 5 -- 5D01010.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't seem to have the electronic version of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may correct something. My father did not contact this office. This office contacted my father because, up until that time, they didn't have any information on the names of the people who had gone missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I have nothing against such an interpretation. Everything is fine, although I believe in yesterday's transcript something else was said, but it's not necessary to go into that. If we could have a look at the following document, the next document. I have a sufficient number of hard copies here. This is a certificate from that very same office, issued on the 11th of July, 1992, and this certificate confirms that a significant number of Muslim civilians who were detained in Bileca were exchanged. And the office then mentions the necessity of distributing humanitarian aid. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And then it also says that this office holds it necessary and suggests that the above-named persons should be given priority and protection in the following three months in obtaining social medical aid and movement permissions. Can we agree that this office, opened by the HVO, assisted Muslims exchanged -- who were exchanged and who were from Eastern Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could this document please be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are asking for the two documents to be admitted into evidence; is that right? No objection to the text, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was sure of it. Two numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. 5D01010 and 5D010111. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, let's go back to the same subject. You said that most of the people who were exchanged from Eastern Herzegovina had been provided with accommodation in Mostar. Where exactly? Could you be more precise? Was it in a sports hall or was it in flats?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many people were provided with accommodation in the pupils' home, and a significant number of them were provided with accommodation in flats. These people agreed to stay in destroyed flats in eastern part of Mostar, and as a result, they tried to repair these flats to a certain extent, and some of them found accommodation in Western Mostar, in the western part of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: There was more accommodation available there?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And I also have to say that many of those people, including the people who were expelled from Podvelezje in Chetnik operations, many of these people were somewhat afraid of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, during that period of time, summer 1992 and in the autumn, who distributed the flats? Who would assign flats that had been abandoned by JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't just JNA officers but also Serbian civilians. They were the only civilian authorities in Mostar at the time. The HVO represented both the military and civilian authority in Mostar. This was probably on the basis of an agreement from the end of April. I only heard about this, I didn't see it myself, but it was an agreement with the SDA and the HDZ. I can't provide you with any specific details about this because I'm not familiar with the case, but I know that the HVO had both civilian and military power in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Very well. To simplify things, the HVO provided refugees from Eastern Herzegovina with aid through the intermediary of this office, and they then allowed them to find accommodation in flats?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yesterday you said on page 31 of the transcript, line 8, that some of the refugees from Eastern Herzegovina were provided with accommodation in Vranica as well.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A certain number of people were provided with accommodation in Vranica, but they were from the eastern or, rather, left bank, from the area of Brankovci and Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yesterday, you also said, on page 15 and 16 of the transcript, that up until the time the 4th Corps of the BH army was formed in November, 1992 -- you said that this corps was formed because there were more people arriving from Eastern Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about the same people who were exchanged in July and August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So these people were exchanged, and they were mostly Muslims. You said they were exchanged in July and August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: The HVO office, with Mr. Bosnjak at its head, provided them with assistance or, rather, asked that they be granted a special sort of status, and then they found accommodation in Mostar. They found accommodation in flats that the HVO distributed, and then they found positions in the BH army.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's true to an extent. I don't know why you're surprised. Some of them arrived although they hadn't been detained in camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mostly from Pod Vresinje and Podvelezje, and some of them also came from Gacka. They had forced their way through to Mostar. But there were also many people who found positions or became -- or joined the HVO, and I don't see why it should be surprising to say that some of them joined the army, or the "armija."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Today, you said that you weren't a traditional secretary. You weren't a normal secretary. You also had other matters to do with, the social welfare of members of companies, battalions, brigades, and of corps.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: With regard to the office led by Mr. Bosnjak, the office whose responsibility it was to help members of the ABiH, were you aware of the fact that they didn't only help civilians but also members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that at the time they were also treated in the Safet Mujic hospital. Many members of the army were treated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about treatment. I'm talking about social help provided by this office to ABiH members. Are you aware of this since you were involved in such matters?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of the fact, but I must also add that many people were referred to the Red Crescent, and armija or army members would receive humanitarian aid from our warehouses. You'll now say that this came from Croatia again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show us the following document: Document number 5D010019.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could counsel avoid overlapping with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we don't have an electronic version, I have a hard copy. I apologise. It probably won't affect the fact that the e-court isn't functioning, but number should be 5D01009 and not 0019. So a mistake has been made in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, have you had a look at the document?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know who the person concerned is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So you know who the person concerned is. Excellent. So we can then agree that at the beginning of September, 1992, the HVO office in Mostar issued a certificate confirming that the son of Ibro Zlomusica, if I'm reading this correctly, from Podvelezje --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think his name was Nerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: It says he was killed as a member of the 1st Mostar Brigade. And then it says: "This certificate is issued with the aim of giving priority to the family of the killed person and providing social, medical and other kinds of humanitarian aid." Is that correct? You say you know that person.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I do. His brother worked with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Give the number in English. It will be faster.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It will be in English. [In English] 5D01009. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, to conclude with this matter, can you tell us how many people came to Mostar from Eastern Herzegovina in the spring and summer of 1992? I'm referring to those expelled, naturally.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I assume that there were about 10 to 15.000 people who arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: According to the information I have, the number is significantly larger. But even if we agreed that it was the number that you have mentioned, would you be able to tell us anything about the ethnic group or ethnic groups that those people belonged to?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, they were Muslims; they were Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Since you have said you don't have any specific military knowledge, I'm not going to show you any documents that refer to military matters and how things developed in military terms towards the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993. But as a secretary and someone who spend her entire life in Mostar, you are certainly in a position to evaluate what the psychological situation was, or, rather, what the atmosphere was like in the ABiH or in the circles that you moved in. On a number of occasions reference was made to tension in April and May, 1993. Unfortunately, you never mentioned whether, as the commander's secretary, you were aware of the fact that in mid-April in 1993, in the area of Konjic, concern conflicts, certain fights broke out between Muslims and Croats. Let's simplify matters.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I only had hearsay information about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about the slaughter in Trusina, for example?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You didn't? Now, those events in mid-1993, or, rather, in April, 1993, did they lead to any reaction in the headquarters of the brigade and corps, or shouldn't I be asking that in view of the fact that you said that you didn't hear about it?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard about it later, but at that time I really didn't, although I did know that there were tensions, and I do know that since in Konjic, in addition to the brigade -- well, I can't remember the date when the 6th Corps was actually established, but I think it was quite some time later, but anyway, what I know is this: I know that Mr. Pasalic went up there for negotiations of some kind with Duga Covic, and I know that there was an HVO unit up there. As for Trusina, no, I didn't know about that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could the name of Trusina be included in the record? I think that should be at the beginning of page 118, line 4, because this was a very serious crime that took place there, it had serious repercussions on the mood of the Croats in BH and was, of course, reflected on what was to follow. So the name is Trusina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Ms. Drljevic, several times today we mentioned -- or, rather, my colleague Mr. Kovacic, the Defence counsel of Mr. Praljak, showed you documents dated to the second half of April, 1993, about an attempt to reach an agreement. You will remember having seen that a moment ago. We saw a joint communique by Pasalic and Zelenika.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So within the framework of all that, of the attempt to quell the situation, to calm tensions, negotiations were conducted, and one side informed the other side about the capacities that they had at their disposal, both in terms of manpower and materiel and equipment. So I wouldn't ask you that were it not for the fact that in your statements you said that the commander, Hujka, withheld information about the materiel and technical equipment of the HVO, MTS. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that, but I'm not quite sure whether this was not carried out. I know he was angry about it, but I can't say with any certainty whether or not everything went out as a corps decision or a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us why Commander Hujka would withhold information of that kind? Why was it important for that information to remain secret?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't answer that, unfortunately. We can't ask him any more either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, a moment ago, we mentioned medical treatment for members of the BH army. Would you agree that all the hospitals, all the hospital capacities in Mostar, were situated on the right bank of the river Neretva?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And what about the civilians, Muslim civilians and members of the BH army? Were they able to avail themselves of medical treatment in those hospitals without any impediments?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the hospitals were staffed largely by doctors who were Muslims and Bosniaks. And during a certain period of time, they had to take an oath of office as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So they worked until the conflict broke out in May, 1995 [sic]; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and even after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know anything about the preparations for building a hospital or more hospital facilities on the banks of the -- eastern banks of the river Neretva?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already in August, 1992, in South Camp we had outpatients departments and clinics, makeshift clinics for providing first aid. We had a dental service and things like that. And when -- and this was sometime in November or December when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. President, but there seems to be, in line 8 on page 120, a reference to 1995, and I'm not sure if that's correct or if that needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. President. It was 1993. I apologise if I made a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, may we continue with what we were discussing. You were saying that in November, December --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there was increased artillery fire from Chetnik units targeting Mostar, including the dam at the HM Mostar, it was very difficult to carry people across the old bridge by carrying them. That was the only communication between the left and right bank. So what was done was to set up a hospital in the institute of hygiene. I think that that was in 1993, but I'm not quite sure when. I specifically remember -- well, I don't know when that young man was wounded and he was left without his legs. He was wounded at the dam. They returned him to South Camp, but by the time they had taken him across the bridge, they had to amputate both his legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So the fact that Hujka withheld information about materiel and technical equipment and the plans for building a hospital in eastern Mostar has nothing to do with any possible preparations for stopping the alliance, from breaking the alliance?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, according to your testimony yesterday, on page 31, lines 23 and 24, you said that -- and I think this was something that was also brought up today by a colleague of mine. You said that the BH army, on the eastern bank of the river Neretva, had a forward command post in the SDK social accounting services building.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that the headquarters and Main Staff of the corps was in the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us what the distance is between the SDK on the eastern banks of the Neretva and Vranica on the west, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about as the crow flies, but it's quite a long way away if you had to walk because you had to cross the old bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us as the crow flies, roughly, a rough estimate? Give or take 200 metres or 500 metres? It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Right. So it was two kilometres from the headquarters and the forward command post; right? Now, we're talking about the beginning of May, 1993. How far were the JNA forces or Chetnik forces away from the town of Mostar? At what distance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jonjic, I do have to intervene, because there's a question of relevance. I believe that you want to draw up the whole history of 1991, 1992, and 1993 through this witness. Remember the scope of the cross-examination under Rule 90 is such that you have to put your questions as arising from the questions put in examination-in-chief. I have kept quiet so far, but you could put some questions to some other witnesses who are more relevant. This witness is a secretary of the Mostar Battalion. She was a victim. If you want to put sort of geopolitical questions to her or questions of military strategy, it doesn't seem to be right. It's out of place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. I've understood your guidelines and will move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, you were, right up until you were captured in the Vranica building, you worked there on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did civilians live in the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the headquarters of the brigade or, rather, the corps, that the question was ever raised of whether the fact that the headquarters were located in the building in which there were civilians whether those civilians were, by that same token, taken into -- turned into potential victims or hostages?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: That question never arose?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: There were women and children living there as well, were there not?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, with your permission, may I be allowed to say the following: It was a location agreed upon earlier on with the HVO, before I arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Well, I see no reason for me to enter into polemics about that with you because previously the Defence of General Praljak showed documents dated the 21st and 23rd of April, 1993, from which we can see that it was agreed that the BH army should withdraw to South Camp and the military police of the BH army should remain in the existing facilities. So in those documents, there was no provision for the fact that Vranica should remain the headquarters. But that is something that you and I need not discuss here and now. With your permission, Ms. Drljevic, I should like now to talk about the time when you were taken prisoner. The individuals who were taken away with you to the MUP building, you spoke about that at length yesterday, were they -- I'm talking about the journalists. Were they members of the BH army or not?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three of them, no, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And who was, then?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a man who was not captured then, but he was the editor in the radio, and he was assistant commander for moral guidance. His name was Alija Idar [phoen]. And he was brought in subsequently because one of the women had left and she indicated the place where they were hiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I'd like for a moment to return to something that a number of my colleagues asked you about when you changed into civilian clothing. Now, in view of the fact that you and most of the BH army members changed into civilian clothing and that your headquarters were located in a building that was principally a civilian building, did it enter any of your heads that you were putting civilians at risk, that they could be captured as well and detained?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When from the Main Staff they offered that civilians be handed over, because we were accused of holding civilians over the radio, we offered people the chance of going outside, of leaving. Nobody wanted to leave. Even a woman who gave birth the very next day refused to leave. Perhaps somebody will be able to explain this to you more closely, but I didn't hide this at all. I stated how the matter was straight away. And my decision to change into other clothing was not because of -- because I wanted to mask the fact that I was a soldier. Everybody knew that I was a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Well, you confirmed that you changed your clothes and put on civilian clothing. You also said that that was because you were bleeding.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And you said, not without pride - and I respect your pride there - that upon arrival in the Kamena building or the MUP building, that you said straight away that you were a member of the BH army, which some other people didn't do and kept quiet about it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about the others. There were no others there then. There were no other men there. And it was pointless for me not to state that, because the young man who had been taken prisoner during the conflicts a few days before that, and he had a scar on his face, although I didn't know who he was, I think he was arrested, and there was a discussion about these exchanges and the conflicts and so on, and I had already been accommodated over there. He recognised me, so he knew I was a member of the BH army, as did Bozo Pavlovic later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that the first individual whom you met when you arrived in the MUP building was Tihomir Kragulj?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You said that you had had a cup of coffee with him a few days before that. That's what you say on the transcript page 41, lines 14 to 16.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Now, as this man Kragulj met you and, according to what you told us, he said, "Your time is up, Secretary." So you couldn't have kept it quiet about your being a BH army member, because this man Kragulj knew you.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's right. And I didn't try either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not want to keep it quiet. I said I was a member of the army before that, the BH army, before I went out and saw Tihomir there. The first person I recognised was Tihomir Kragulj.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And you said that in the MUP building you were interrogated by Marin Jurica's brother, whose name is Davor, or something like that. And he was a member of the civilian police force, was he, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he was at that time but I think he was an investigator or an interrogator before the war as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: After Mostar, that is to say after you spent some time in Mostar -- tell us how far Ljubuski is away from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Roughly.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps some 30 or 40 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that assessment. I know very well what the distance is, but you said that it took you an hour or two to get there, and that's on page 46 of the transcript, lines 11 to 12. Can you tell us why this journey of 30 or so kilometres lasted an hour or two?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we drove in a column, and perhaps I didn't make the right assessment. We didn't stop off along the way anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You said that in front of the military investigative prison in Ljubuski, you saw a line of soldiers in black uniforms. I'm quoting.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did these soldiers have any insignia?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say. One of them ordered us to stand up against the wall and to spread our arms and legs apart, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: But you're sure that the uniforms were black?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some of the uniforms. They were mixed uniforms. I get sick from black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, on page 47, line 15 to 17, of the transcript, you said that in prison in Ljubuski there were truck drivers from Bosnia who were not imprisoned but were free there.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: What did you mean by that, they were free?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that somewhere in another building but also in that building where we were but at another room, they spent the night there, and during daytime they could move about the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Did you see these people?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I talked to one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what their ethnic background was?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Muslims, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: When you spoke to some of them, were you able to establish how old they were?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was referring to the man whom I saw there, whom I knew before the war from Tuzla. He also didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: What was his age, roughly?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 45 to 50. His name is Mirsad. I don't know his last name. In Tuzla, he was director of Univerzalpromet. I used to work with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So he was of an age group which normally is considered fit to serve in the army.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that they had gone to buy some supplies. His company deals with publishing mostly, so they needed whatever was needed for bookshops and publishing company, and they went to get supplies and then got stuck there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So he was fit to serve in the army, he was a Muslim, and he was there. He was detained but not imprisoned; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You said in your statements and yesterday when giving evidence that the status of female inmates in Ljubuski was a decent one due to correct conduct of Santic and Prlic.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You just helped me. For years I couldn't remember his first name, Santic's first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: How did you acquire this information about the different status of male inmates?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that yesterday. Once they allowed me to take cigarettes to them, and some extra food that was left from lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And where did you get cigarettes?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave those people from Bosnia -- I asked them to get cigarettes for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: All right. So because they were able to go into town, they were able to get cigarettes for you. Did they have to go through some checks upon return? Were they searched?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well -- but I asked the commander prior to that for permission to buy cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the usher's assistance. Document 5D01002.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, can you read this document? This is the order of the Stjepan Radic Brigade, headquartered in Ljubuski, whereby the military police is ordered to take certain steps concerning the treatment of inmates in prison in Ljubuski. It is stated that all prisoners, male and female, have the same status while in detention. And item 5 says that they need to be treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. Ms. Drljevic, this was on the 18th of May, 1993. So it is quite clear that this order pertained to you as well. I'm interested in item 4, whether it pertains to the journalists who had come from Vranica. Were there any other journalists there?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most likely it pertains to journalists from Vranica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: There were not any other journalists there?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I also offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This will be in English. [In English] 5D01002. [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jonjic, how much time do you need? Because after you we'll have Mr. Ibrisimovic, then we'll have additional questions by the Prosecution, possibly questions by the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Mr. President. I will not conclude within half an hour, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, if you need another half hour, the witness will have to come back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will leave it up to the Chamber to rule on this. I have a number of questions pertaining to the conditions in Ljubuski and Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Well, put your questions if you deem them relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, you said that you arrived in Ljubuski with your bleeding still in progress and that Dr. Suko treated you. What kind of medical assistance were you able to get there in Ljubuski? Were you able to ask for treatment? Were you able to go to the infirmary?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask for any treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether you would have been assisted had you asked for assistance?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: On page 53 and 54 of the transcript, you said that in Ljubuski you were registered by the ICRC after 10 days -- 10 days after your arrival, which would have been the 23rd, 24th.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, on the 25th. And you can see that in the certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned several times that the representatives of the International Red Cross encountered problems in entering the prison. So could we please see document 5D01001. Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So this is an order of the commander of the operation zone, Mr. Lasic, approving -- approving it for the International Red Cross to once again visit prisons, including those in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I ask that this document be admitted into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This will be Exhibit [In English] 5D01001. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll try to accelerate the pace and abbreviate as much as possible. I'm sure that Ms. Drljevic is quite tired too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, we now turn to Heliodrom. In your statements, you mentioned that you and other inmates were asked to look at the list of prisoners and to circle the names of the army members.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When interrogated by a person who introduced himself and who had an ID with a photograph, the one that is attached but not the one that is opened. The name stated on that ID was Josip Vrdoljak. I don't know whether that was the real name of that person or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can it be concluded, based on that, that the members of the BH army could not be distinguished based on their uniforms, because all of them had changed into civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to September.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: To Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I came to Heliodrom in June, and you're now speaking of September. Everybody who was there was there in civilian clothes. Those who wore uniforms are missing, and nobody said anything about their fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: All right. This wasn't clear, but we don't have enough time to go into that today. On page 17, line 18 to 20, of the transcript, you said that the ICRC was allowed to enter Heliodrom only in September of 1993.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: All right. In August. You weren't there in May, but you said explicitly that this had been confirmed to you by a person who was there from the 10th of May but wasn't registered until August.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Based on which you concluded that the ICRC did not go to Heliodrom before August at all.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this person spent some time in solitary confinement, it is possible, but starting from the 8th of June and for the following two months there were no visits of the Red Cross. I cited the example of that person who was brought there in May but wasn't registered until August.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see document 5D01004.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you see this document, Ms. Drljevic? This is a letter from Mr. Darinko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Sent to the International Red Cross in Split, whereby he informs them that, due to security reasons, some 1.500 persons, mostly Muslims, were put in Heliodrom near Mostar. This document is dated 10th of May, 1993. Is it possible that the person you spoke to wasn't registered and that the Red Cross was denied access there? So is it possible, is it plausible when the HVO itself appealed to them to receive various supplies, including blankets and so on?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That person was not registered, that's for certain. I don't know why. Maybe the Red Cross didn't want to go there. What is peculiar is this phrase here, "due to security reasons."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I tender this document into evidence as well, and I will reduce my questions to just two more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure if it's a translation issue or perhaps from the document, but we can't see any indications on the document that it's actually dated 10 May, 1993, at least on the English translation. My learned colleague, on line 10, indicates it's dated the 10th of May. I don't seem to see that, at least on the document as it's currently visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us on what basis you can say that the date is the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the Croatian original, in the upper right corner it says the 10th of May. Now, whether this is fully reliable or not, that's hard to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. I note that in the Croatian document I can see 10/05/93. Please proceed. You have another two questions. First the number, right. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] 5D01004.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Just two more outstanding questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, when speaking of medical treatment at Heliodrom, you mentioned Necko Hadzic, Mirsad Stranjak, as physicians, and also a male nurse called Corojevic.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You also spoke of being taken to the military clinic to receive IV fluids.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: The doctors you mentioned, maybe you know them personally or maybe you can conclude that based on their names; what is their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, how was medical care organised at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally a doctor would come if some of us had complaints about not feeling well. Or when I had this problem with my back, for example, they came. When called, they came immediately. Perhaps some other people might have a different opinion, but my experience is that the doctors and medical staff treated women very properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My final question: I don't think we need to go into private session. You spoke today of your own health problems which led you to have amnesia and so on. Can you tell us, what were the reasons for that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that that was in September and October of 1993. October of 1993. I'm now trying to remember this. The fact that I was taken away caused me to suffer terrible stress, and the weapons too. Let me tell you this: I wasn't afraid at Vranica. You knew you could get killed when people were shooting, but in this other situation, when there were other women there, that was quite a stress.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: My last question: Can we, based on that, conclude that your testimony and your claims about all of the events after September and October should be treated with a lot of reservation in view of your health condition?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think so. I talked to doctors about this, especially with Dr. Hrvic, who is a forensic expert and has been to The Hague to testify. I also spoke to Dr. Curic and Dr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Mehmed Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Mehmed Kovacevic was also detained somewhere.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Dretelj, and he got diabetes there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Ibrisimovic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I don't know what the schedule is now, because the witness is tired, but I don't have many questions for the witness, and I think that the time remaining should be sufficient for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Drljevic, I only have a few questions. I believe you are tired. I won't go into detail. My questions have to do with what you said about the 8th of June, 1993, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On page 61 of the transcript, you said that you then saw Mr. Marcinko.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Marcinko.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And you said, "I knew that he was a high-ranking officer in the military police"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously the military and the civilian authorities were intertwined. I really don't know exactly which authority was concerned, but I think it was the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said he was at the school of mechanical engineering.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that Mr. Marcinko told you you were going to the Heliodrom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You then spoke to Mr. Pusca [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you spoke to Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the room that we were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You and Mr. Pusic spoke about your relatives, about some common friends, acquaintances, and I believe that this was an informal conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He also said that the reason for being moved there was that we should soon be released and sent home. It had been decided that everyone should be placed in the vicinity of their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So this wasn't an official conversation that you had between you and Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're correct. I don't really know what capacity he was there in, but he wasn't part of that brigade that had issued prohibition on communication. He had probably come there officially. But it's quite obvious that the conversation was a private one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: According to the tone used or mentioned, you could say that he was friendly?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, it doesn't say that Mr. Pusic greeted you on behalf of your family, on behalf of a relative of yours.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just wanted to clarify these circumstances surrounding the conversation that the witness had with Mr. Pusic on the 8th of June. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have no further questions. Mr. Mundis, do you have additional questions, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said possibly, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
