utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I know that it's very tiring to testify for two days. I personally will only have a few brief questions that are directly connected to your statement of yesterday and today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday you were asked by the Prosecutor to describe the armed forces present in Mostar, and you stated that there was the Spanish Battalion, the HVO, and the ABiH, and I believe I understood that you said that there was also the Croatian army. Could you be more specific on this? Is it possible that there were parts of the Croatian army present in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that concerns the people I went to see in front of the pensioner's hotel, which is now called Hotel Ero. There were a lot of people who were speaking in this Dalmatian accent, which isn't an accent that you hear in our area, not even in Western Herzegovina. I didn't see any insignia on them, but I also based this conclusion on the testimony of other women, on the basis of what other women said who went to work. They said that -- well, they knew which buildings the units from the Tigers and Thunder were from -- were in, and on the 15th of July I saw some identity cards of members of the Croatian army from Split and Osijek, members who had been killed. I saw that later on. But an old woman and her daughter-in-law later told me something that happened on the 13th of July, 1992. She said that a large number of members of the Croatian army from Split and Osijek died in that area. There is a chapel located in that area now. As far as the people who had set off from the direction of the stadium, the Velez stadium, are concerned, I can't really say where they came from. Perhaps from Croatia, but perhaps from Western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have a Croat from Croatia and a Croat from Bosnia and Herzegovina, can you make a distinction as to their accents?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To large extent. To a large extent it's possible to make such a distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to understand you well. So if you have a Croat from Zagreb, he will speak differently from a Croat from Croatia but who is in Bosnia and Herzegovina? You can hear the difference, can you?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's now a little more difficult to make such a distinction, but at the time it was easy since everyone is now trying to speak a very pure Croatian language. Those who were born in Mostar now have a sort of mixed accent, but it's nevertheless possible to recognise a Zagreb accent and a Mostar Zagrebian accent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us that in Heliodrom you were in a room in the attic or under the roof and that on the first floor there was a partition or a -- between the people -- the HVO people who were detained, that they were in one part, and in the other part there were people from Mostar. You said that very quickly. This is the reason why I'd like to sort of have further information of this. You said that the deputy commander of the Ljubuski prison, Mr. Santic, had been brought there. So I asked myself, was he detained as well and, if so, why, or did he just pay a visit to Heliodrom? Could you be more specific on this.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I knew about this because it's something I had heard from people who were there. There were two or three individuals who were free in a certain sense. They were prisoners, but they weren't kept in cells. So then I asked them, and they answered the question. Later on I heard from the men that they would sometimes let them out. When you go up onto the floor, there were people from Mostar on one side, mostly from Mostar, and there were some people from Mostar in half of the -- on the ground floor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I understood all that. I wanted to know from you whether the deputy commander of the Ljubuski prison was detained, imprisoned in Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He personally said that that was the case, and the guard Marjanovic also told me that that was the case. I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know why he was detained?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because -- well, I asked him before he was released. He spent seven days there, I think. On one occasion he came and asked me whether I needed anything. He brought some cigarettes and some fruit. I really didn't know that man from before, and I never saw him after that event. And then the guard Marjanovic grew angry. I asked him not to come again. As a result, I knew that he was an officer. He said that two prisoners had escaped, had managed to escape from him, and that is why he had been imprisoned for seven or eight days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked you why he had been in prison, why he had been detained.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because two of his prisoners in Ljubuski had escaped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was then imprisoned in the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, when speaking of the people detained in Heliodrom, you mentioned names, you gave their ages, and at a different point in time you mentioned a lady who was with her two children, and you said that when the Red Cross came, this woman and her two children were taken somewhere - I don't know where - and that they came back. Do you remember exactly that situation of a mother with two children who would have left Heliodrom because of the Red Cross coming and that they would have come back later? Could you be more precise on this?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't a mother. It was Nena and her two grandchildren. When she returned, they said they had moved her to a house. It was this grandmother and they then took her to a different house. I found out about that when leaving the camp. They weren't registered, they're not on that list, on the Red Cross's list. And there were also two women with two daughters. One was a young girl, 17 or 18 years old -- I don't really know how old she was. And the other girl was only 9 years old. And then there was the son Narcis. He was 15 or 16 years old. He was in the male part of the prison. I don't know whether he was released in December or in March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question: In the afternoon you mentioned that apparently a film was made, and I say it your language; "Grbavica," and you said that following this you were under pressure. You were put under pressure. What did you mean? Did they make a film of the events? Did you -- what facts do you remember in regard to this movie named Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a film that was shown at the festival in Berlin and received some sort of prize. It is about a woman -- it is about a woman who was raped and she got pregnant as a result, and this is something that affected me a lot because it was always a short of threat that I felt. Luckily, I didn't have such an experience, but I do react to such things in this way. Therapy helps, but it's also obvious that fatigue contributes to my state. I mentioned Grbavica because it brings everything back. My doctor says this is a flashback, and I have these images that return to me occasionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak. You wanted to say something? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] The film received the Golden Bear in Berlin, and acts of rape committed by the Serbs in Central Bosnia were filmed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I think that that makes no difference. The woman is raped. A woman is also a human being, and it doesn't matter what her name is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Following the questions by the Judges, do you have any further questions, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, my understanding is that the practice would be for us to be entitled to go last, following any follow-up questions from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you please. Any questions by the Defence counsel following my questions? No, there isn't. Very well. You have completed your testimony. Thank you for testifying for two days and answering questions by the Prosecution, by all the Defence counsel, and me. Thank you for coming to testify. I shall ask the usher to take you back to your room outside this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have another witness tomorrow. I remind you of the fact that the Prosecution spent 282 minutes, the Defence 253 minutes, the Judges 14 minutes. Mr. Mundis, what about your witness today? What do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Tomorrow, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We fully expect to have the witness that's on the schedule for tomorrow morning here and available, commencing at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I ask how long they intend to take on the direct examination, just so we can plan ahead, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was my question, the question nagging me. Mr. Mundis, for the Defence to usefully prepare their cross-examination, tell us how long you will take.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, my recollection is that the 65 ter estimate for the witness is four and a half hours. My colleague Mr. Scott will actually be conducting the direct examination. He informs me that he's hopeful he can do it in four hours. Given that tomorrow is a six-hour day and then a normal merely four-hour day on Friday, we would hope that we can finish this witness by the end of the week and that he wouldn't have to then stay over until Monday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. Four hours for the Prosecution, and you will have the end of tomorrow's hearing and Friday morning until quarter to two. This is for all the Defence counsel. I know it's not easy at all to coordinate your work among yourselves, because sometimes you have to ask the same questions or similar questions. Again, this happened today, about this labour contract. But I think that as time goes by everybody is going to improve on their performance when it comes to putting questions, and this will be very useful for everybody. Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Praljak, for this information you gave us. Let us convene again tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
